<<Q_RELEVANT>>In December 2006, Capital One acquired its GreenPoint Mortgage unit when the company paid $13.2 billion for North Fork Bancorp Inc.[64] During the subprime mortgage crisis, Capital One closed its mortgage platform, GreenPoint Mortgage, due in part to investor pressures, cutting 1,900 jobs and costing the company $860 million in charges.[65][66][67] The U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Securities and Exchange Commission criticized Capital One's conduct during the crisis, claiming that they understated auto loan losses during the 2008 financial crisis.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2013, Capital One paid $3.5 million to settle the case, but was not required to directly address the allegations of wrongdoing.[68] In 2008, Capital One received an investment of $3.56 billion from the United States Treasury as a result of the Troubled Asset Relief Program.[69][70] On June 17, 2009, Capital One completed the repurchase of the stock the company issued to the U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Treasury paying a total of $3.67 billion, resulting in a profit of over $100 million to the U.S. Treasury.[71]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1996, Capital One expanded its business operations to the United Kingdom and Canada.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This gave the company access to a large international market for its credit cards. An article appearing in Chief Executive in 1997 noted that the company held $12.6 billion in credit card receivables and served more than nine million customers. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The company was listed in the Standard & Poor's 500, and its stock price hit the $100 mark for the first time in 1998.[18]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2005 Capital One became the first monoline credit card issuer to buy a bank, as it entered into retail banking by acquiring Hibernia National Bank.[31] It purchased the New Orleans, Louisiana-based Hibernia for $4.9 billion in cash and stock.[32] It acquired Melville, New York-based North Fork Bank for $13.2 billion in cash and stock in 2006.[33] The acquisition of retail banks greatly reduced its dependency on the credit-card business alone.[34] It briefly considered acquiring Netspend, a marketer of prepaid debit cards, for $700 million in 2007, but the deal was not ultimately completed.[35]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In February 2009, Capital One acquired Chevy Chase Bank for $520 million in cash and stock.[37][38][39][40]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In August 2011, Capital One reached a deal with HSBC to acquire its U.S. credit card operations.[44] Capital One paid $31.3 billion in exchange for $28.2 billion in loans and $600 million in other assets.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The acquisition was completed in May 2012.[45] The acquisition also included private issued credit cards for such companies as Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Lord & Taylor that were previously handled by HSBC.[46]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2012, Capital One closed 41 branch locations.[49]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2014, Capital One amended its terms of use to allow it to "contact you in any manner we choose", including a "personal visit . . . at your home and at your place of employment".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It also asserted its right to "modify or suppress caller ID and similar services and identify ourselves on these services in any manner we choose".[50] The company stated that it would not actually make personal visits to customers except "As a last resort, . . . if it becomes necessary to repossess [a] sports vehicle".[50] Capital One also attributed its assertion of a right to "spoof" as necessary because "sometimes the number is 'displayed differently' by 'some local phone exchanges,' something that is 'beyond our control'".[51]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2015, Capital One closed several branch locations to leave 174 operating branches in the D.C. metro area.[56]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The re-emergence into the mortgage industry came in June 2011, when ING Group announced the sale of its ING Direct division to Capital One for $9 billion in cash and stock.[72][73] On August 26, 2011, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors announced it would hold public hearings on the Capital One acquisition of ING Direct, and extend to October 12, 2011, the public comment period that had been scheduled to end August 22.[74] The move came amidst rising scrutiny of the deal on systemic risk, or "Too-Big-to-Fail," performance under the Community Reinvestment Act, and pending legal challenges.<</Q_RELEVANT>> A coalition of national civil rights and consumer groups, led by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, were joined by Rep. Barney Frank to challenge immediate approval of the deal. The groups argued that the acquisition was a test of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, under which systemically risky firms must demonstrate a public benefit that outweighs new risk before they are allowed to grow. Kansas City Federal Reserve Bank head Thomas M. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Hoenig was also skeptical of the deal.[75][76] In February 2012, the acquisition was approved by regulators and Capital One completed its acquisition of ING Direct.[77] Capital One received permission to merge ING into its business in October 2012,[78] and rebranded ING Direct as Capital One 360 in November 2012.[79]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.text:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>On June 17, 1983, Amgen became a public company via an initial public offering, selling two million common shares and raising nearly $40 million.[10][11][12] That same year, after more than two years of work, an Amgen research team led by Fu-Kuen Lin found and cloned the erythropoietin gene, a protein created in the kidney that stimulates red blood cell production.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Lin's team created what would become Epogen (epoetin alfa).[13][14]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In October 1988, Gordon Binder was named CEO, succeeding George Rathmann.[19] The following year, in 1989, Amgen received approval for the first recombinant human erythropoetin product, Epogen (epoetin alfa).[20]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The company's major products are Prolia and XGEVA (Denosumab) for treatment of osteoporosis and bone diseases ($6.7 billion in total 2024 revenues), Enbrel (Etanercept) for treatment of autoimmune diseases ($3.3 billion in 2024 revenues), Repatha (evolocumab) for treatment of hyperlipidemia ($2.3 billion in 2024 revenues), Otezla (apremilast) for treatment of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis ($2.1 billion in 2024 revenues), Tepezza (teprotumumab) to treat Graves' ophthalmopathy ($1.8 billion in 2024 revenues), Evenity (romosozumab) to treat osteoporosis ($1.5 billion in 2024 revenues), Kyprolis (carfilzomib) to treat cancer ($1.5 billion in 2024 revenues), Nplate (romiplostim) to regulate platelet production ($1.4 billion in 2024 revenues), and Aranesp (darbepoetin alfa) to stimulate erythropoiesis ($1.3 billion in 2024 revenues).[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Amgen Inc. is an American multinational biopharmaceutical company headquartered in Thousand Oaks, California.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The company is ranked 18th on the list of largest biomedical companies by revenue. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The name "AMGen" is a portmanteau of the company's original name, Applied Molecular Genetics.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In April 1980, Amgen was founded in Thousand Oaks as Applied Molecular Genetics.[6] Amgen was backed by a small group of venture capitalists, and its early focus was on recombinant DNA technology and recombinant human insulin.[7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Amgen Inc. (Founded 1983 as Applied Molecular Genetics)<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Amgen Inc. v.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Harris, a United States Supreme Court case on employment law.

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Amgen Inc v.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Sanofi, a United States Supreme Court case on patent enablement.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Amgen has 17 clinical programs underway in Phase III, eight in Phase II, and 19 in Phase I.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Its pipeline includes MariTide, an anti-obesity medication administered once per month by injection.[2]

Its initial scientific advisory board consisted of Norman Davidson, Leroy Hood, Arnold Berk, John Carbon, Robert Schimke, Arno Motulsky, Marvin H. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Caruthers, and Dave Gibson.[8] In October 1980, Amgen named George Rathmann its first president and chief executive officer.[7][9]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 1984, Amgen and Kirin Brewery Company formed a joint venture giving Kirin the rights to Epogen in Japan, while Amgen retained United States distribution rights; both companies had the opportunity to expand to other countries.[15]  This joint venture gave way in 2017 to a new joint venture, Kirin-Amgen, which bought out Kirin Holdings stake.[16]  A year later, Amgen researcher Larry Souza and his team cloned granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), leading to the development of Neupogen (filgrastim).[14][17][18]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In February 1991, Amgen received FDA approval for Neupogen for the prevention of infections in patients whose immune systems are suppressed due to cancer chemotherapy.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Amgen opened a new manufacturing facility in Puerto Rico, in March 1993, which later became the company's flagship manufacturing site.[22]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1994, Amgen became the fifth company to receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation from the United States Department of Commerce, in recognition of its work developing medicines to improve quality of life for kidney and cancer patients.[23] Also around this time, Amgen researcher Steve Elliott and his team added more sugar molecules to erythropoietin, causing it to remain in the body longer.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This led to the development of Aranesp (darbepoetin alfa).[24]

Binder was succeeded as CEO by Kevin W. Sharer in 2000.[25] Robert A. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Bradway became Amgen's president and chief executive officer in May 2012, following Sharer's retirement.[26]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 2010, Amgen received approval by the Food and Drug Administration for Prolia, a protein drug for the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis.[27] In clinical trials, Prolia reduced the rate of vertebral fractures by 61% and the risk of hip fractures by 40%.[28] In November 2010, the FDA approved Xgeva for the prevention of complications of bone metastases in patients with solid tumors.[29] The clinical trials primarily enrolled patients with breast or prostate cancer.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In March 2011, Amgen acquired a manufacturing facility near Dublin, Ireland.[30]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Amgen opened an affiliate in China in 2013.[31][32]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>Baxter International Inc. is an American multinational healthcare company with headquarters in Deerfield, Illinois.[2]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In January, as Baxter International Inc.'s Vernon Loucks relinquished his CEO duties after 18 years, directors handed him a special stock-option grant of 950,000 shares "for the specific purposes of motivating" him "to implement a smooth transition of his responsibilities." If Mr.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Loucks sells all the 400,000 shares he can exercise at year end and Baxter's stock price remains at its current level, he will make more than $4 million.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Baxter's Healthcare System and Technologies business has four divisions "Front Line Care", "Digital Platform and Innovations", "Care and Connectivity Solutions" and "Global Services".<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1996, the company entered into a four-way, $640 million settlement with haemophiliacs 1999 in relation to blood clotting concentrates that were infected with HIV.[17]  Under pressure from shareholders due to poor performance and an unsuccessful merger, Loucks was forced to resign.[13]: 115<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In May 2023, Baxter announced it was selling its biopharma solutions business, which offers drugmakers support in the form of products like injectable delivery systems and services that include regulatory resources, help with drug formulation and development, and packaging capabilities, to private equity firms Warburg Pincus and Advent International for $4.25 billion in cash.[32][33]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Baxter was included for the 13th year in Corporate Responsibility magazine's 100 Best Corporate Citizens list in 2014 for its social responsibility performance.[51]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Baxter International was founded in 1931 by Donald Baxter, a Los Angeles-based medical doctor, as a manufacturer and distributor of intravenous therapy solutions.[3] Seeing a need for products closer to the Midwest, the company opened a manufacturing plant in Glenview, Illinois, in 1933.[3] Baxter's interest was bought out in 1935 by Ralph Falk, who established a research and development function.[4]  In 1939 the company developed a vacuum-type collection container, extending the shelf life of blood from hours to weeks.[4]  In 1954, the company expanded operations outside of the United States by opening an office in Belgium.[5] In 1956 Baxter International introduced the first functioning artificial kidney, and in 1971 became a member of the Fortune 500.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

In March 2014, Baxter announced plans to create two independent global healthcare companies—one focused on developing and marketing bio-pharmaceuticals and the other on medical products. <<QA_RELEVANT>>The medical products company retained the name Baxter International Inc. and the bio-pharmaceuticals company is named Baxalta and spun-off as a new public company that showed on trading boards as of July 1, 2015.[22]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In September 2024, Hurricane Helene caused significant flooding in North Carolina, affecting a Baxter International facility in Marion.<</Q_RELEVANT>> This facility produces approximately 60% of the intravenous (IV) fluids used in the United States. <<A_RELEVANT>>The disruption led to nationwide IV fluid shortages, prompting hospitals to ration supplies and implement strategies to conserve fluids.<</A_RELEVANT>> This also prompted questions from medical professionals about why such a large portion of the country's IV manufacturing capacity is tied to a single facility. As of November 7, 2024, the facility resumed producing some IV fluids. However, with the onset of flu season, hospitals continued to prioritize conservation efforts.[35]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>On July 2, 2009, Kentucky Attorney General Jack Conway announced a settlement between the state and Baxter Healthcare Corporation, a subsidiary of Baxter International, worth $2 million.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The company had been inflating the cost of the intravenous drugs sold to Kentucky Medicaid, at times as much as 1300%.[70]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Business data for Baxter International Inc.: GoogleSEC filingsYahoo!<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>On July 15, 1985, American Hospital Supply Corporation CEO Karl D.<</A_RELEVANT>> Bays and Baxter's then-CEO Vernon R. Loucks Jr. signed an agreement that merged two of the United States' "largest producers of medical supplies".[14] This was a "one-Baxter approach" in which the company provided "70% to 80% of what a hospital needed."[15]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1991, Baxter's home infusion subsidiary, Caremark International, "was accused by the government of paying doctors to steer patients to its intravenous drug service"[16] In 1992 Caremark spun off from Baxter International.[16] Caremark was fined $160 million for the "four-year-long federal mail-fraud and kickback" scheme in which the "home-infusion business unit made weekly payments to scores of doctors that averaged about $75 per patient for referring those patients to its services.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Some doctors earned as much as $80,000 a year from the kickbacks, according to government documents."[16]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Baxter acquired medical device firm Baxa on November 10, 2011.[18] In 2011, Hikma Pharmaceuticals PLC completed the acquisition of Baxter Healthcare Corporation's US generic injectables business (Multi-Source Injectables or MSI).[19][20]<</A_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.text:
In 2015, Target followed Walmart in raising its minimum wage to $9 per hour.[127] Two years later, Target announced that the minimum hourly wage would be increased to $11 by October 2017 and pledged to raise it to $15 (referred to as "living wage" by labor advocates) by 2020.[128][129] By April 2019, the company announced that it was on track to meet this goal, increasing its minimum wage to $13 per hour.[130] In June 2020, Target announced ahead of schedule that the minimum hourly wage would rise to $15 permanently, after previously announcing it to be temporary through July 4, 2020. <<Q_RELEVANT>>As a thank you to store and distribution center team members who worked during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, Target also announced a one-time $200 bonus to be paid towards the end of July 2020.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>During the COVID-19 pandemic, Target began providing additional team member resources to help team members meet essential needs, obtain virtual healthcare, and take a paid leave of absence (based on certain medical or physical criteria that may cause exposure to coronavirus).[131][132] In February 2021, Target began offering all of its hourly employees up to four hours of pay when they get both doses of the COVID-19 vaccine as well as covering the cost of a Lyft ride, up to $15 each way, to the vaccination appointment.[133] In August 2021, Target announced a $200 million investment to offer debt-free degrees to more than 340,000 full-time and part-time team members at stores, distribution centers, and headquarters locations.[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Minneapolis-St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Paul Stock Exchange<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Target Corporation has its headquarters on Nicollet Mall in Minneapolis[75] near the site of the original Goodfellows store.[76] The complex includes Target Plaza North and Target Plaza South.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Ryan Companies developed the complex, and Ellerbe Becket served as the architect. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Target had the roughly $260 million complex developed to provide one location of office space for 6,000 employees.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The 14-story Target Plaza North has 600,000 square feet (56,000 m2) of office and retail space, while the 32-story Target Plaza South has 1,250,000 square feet (116,000 m2) of space.[77] In October 2014, Target completed construction of an 1,600,000 square feet corporate campus in Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, called Target Northern Campus.[78]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Target stores are designed to compete against large big-box stores by having wider aisles, drop ceilings, and their own unique presentation of merchandise. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Graphics around the store reinforce its advertising imagery, while shelves are dressed with contemporary signage, backdrops, and liners, often printed on inexpensive material such as paper, corrugated and foam boards.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some stores, particularly those in the vicinity of major airports, have a bullseye painted on the roof that can be seen from above: the stores in East Point, Georgia, near Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport; Rosemont, Illinois, near O'Hare International Airport; Potomac Yard, Virginia, near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport; College Point, New York (Queens), east of LaGuardia Airport; and Richfield, Minnesota, adjacent to Minneapolis–St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Paul International Airport are among such locations.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The location in Inglewood, California, near Los Angeles International Airport and SoFi Stadium, has an LED bullseye logo on its roof, made out of solar panels.[140]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Target has a no-solicitation rule at its properties, as it seeks to provide a "distraction-free shopping experience for its guests." Exemptions to this policy were previously made for the Salvation Army red kettles and bell-ringers outside Target stores during the holidays through Christmas. In 2004, however, Target asked the organization to explore alternate methods to partner with Target. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Target donates to local Salvation Army chapters through its grant program and annually to the United Way of America (the Salvation Army is a member of the United Way coalition).[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Target Corporation is a major sponsor of the annual Minneapolis Aquatennial, where it hosts the Target Fireworks Show, the largest annual fireworks show west of the Mississippi River and the fourth-largest annual fireworks show in the United States.[213]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Michael Fiddelke serves as CEO of Target Corporation, having succeeded Brian Cornell on February 1, 2026.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Cornell transitioned to the role of executive chairman of the board.[2] Cornell had served as chairman and CEO since 2014.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In January 2016, Cornell began making home visits in an effort to understand better the needs and desires of his customers.[79] In January 2016, Target fired Tina Tyler from her job as chief stores officer. She was replaced with long-time employee Janna Potts.[80]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Officially, Japan has 16 national, government-recognized holidays.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Public holidays in Japan are regulated by the Public Holiday Law (国民の祝日に関する法律, Kokumin no Shukujitsu ni Kansuru Hōritsu) of 1948.[335] Beginning in 2000, Japan implemented the Happy Monday System, which moved a number of national holidays to Monday in order to obtain a long weekend.[336] The national holidays in Japan are New Year's Day on January 1, Coming of Age Day on the second Monday of January, National Foundation Day on February 11, The Emperor's Birthday on February 23, Vernal Equinox Day on March 20 or 21, Shōwa Day on April 29, Constitution Memorial Day on May 3, Greenery Day on May 4, Children's Day on May 5, Marine Day on the third Monday of July, Mountain Day on August 11, Respect for the Aged Day on the third Monday of September, Autumnal Equinox on September 23 or 24, Health and Sports Day on the second Monday of October, Culture Day on November 3, and Labor Thanksgiving Day on November 23.[337]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Japan's legislative organ is the National Diet, a bicameral parliament.[115] It consists of a lower House of Representatives with 465 seats, elected by popular vote every four years or when dissolved, and an upper House of Councillors with 248 seats, whose popularly elected members serve six-year terms.[117] There is universal suffrage for adults over 18 years of age,[118] with a secret ballot for all elected offices.[116] The prime minister as the head of government has the power to appoint and dismiss Ministers of State, and is appointed by the emperor after being designated from among the members of the Diet.[117] Sanae Takaichi is Japan's prime minister; she took office after winning the 2025 Liberal Democratic Party leadership election and securing a confidence and supply agreement with Ishin.[119] The broadly conservative Liberal Democratic Party has been the dominant party in the country since the 1950s, often called the 1955 System.[120]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Besides Japanese, the Ryukyuan languages (Amami, Kunigami, Okinawan, Miyako, Yaeyama, Yonaguni), part of the Japonic language family, are spoken in the Ryukyu Islands chain.[260] Few children learn these languages,[261] but local governments have sought to increase awareness of the traditional languages.[262] The Ainu language, which is a language isolate, is moribund, with only a few native speakers remaining as of 2014[update].[263] Additionally, a number of other languages are taught and used by ethnic minorities, immigrant communities, and a growing number of foreign-language students, such as Korean (including a distinct Zainichi Korean dialect), Chinese, and Portuguese.[257]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Domestic security in Japan is provided mainly by the prefectural police departments, under the oversight of the National Police Agency.[150] As the central coordinating body for the Prefectural Police Departments, the National Police Agency is administered by the National Public Safety Commission.[151] The Special Assault Team comprises national-level counter-terrorism tactical units that cooperate with territorial-level Anti-Firearms Squads and Counter-NBC Terrorism Squads.[152] The Japan Coast Guard guards territorial waters surrounding Japan and uses surveillance and control countermeasures against smuggling, marine environmental crime, poaching, piracy, spy ships, unauthorized foreign fishing vessels, and illegal immigration.[153]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>As of 2019[update], 37.1% of energy in Japan is produced from petroleum, 25.1% from coal, 22.4% from natural gas, 3.5% from hydropower and 2.8% from nuclear power, among other sources.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Nuclear power was down from 11.2% in 2010.[228] By May 2012 all of the country's nuclear power plants had been taken offline because of ongoing public opposition following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster in March 2011, though government officials continued to try to sway public opinion in favor of returning at least some to service.[229] The Sendai Nuclear Power Plant restarted in 2015,[230] and since then several other nuclear power plants have been restarted.[231] Japan lacks significant domestic reserves and has a heavy dependence on imported energy.[232] The country has therefore aimed to diversify its sources and maintain high levels of energy efficiency.[233]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Japanese language is Japan's de facto national language and the primary written and spoken language of most people in the country.[257] Japanese writing uses kanji (Chinese characters) and two sets of kana (syllabaries based on cursive script and radicals used by kanji), as well as the Latin alphabet and Arabic numerals.[258] English has taken a major role in Japan as a business and international link language, and is a compulsory subject at the junior and senior high school levels.[259] Japanese Sign Language is the primary sign language used in Japan and has gained some official recognition, but its usage has been historically hindered by discriminatory policies and a lack of educational support.[257]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Paraguay
entity_document.text:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Paraguay is a representative democratic republic, with a multi-party system and separation of powers across three branches.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Executive power is exercised solely by the President, who is head of state and head of government.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Legislative power is vested in the two chambers of the National Congress. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The judiciary is vested on tribunals and Courts of Civil Law and a nine-member Supreme Court of Justice, all of them independent of the executive and the legislature.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>For most of its history, Paraguay has been a recipient of immigrants owing to its low population density, especially after the demographic collapse caused by the Paraguayan War.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Immigrants include Italians, Germans, Spanish, English, Russians, Koreans, Chinese, Arab, Japanese, Ukrainians, Poles, Jews, Brazilians, Bolivians, Americans, Colombians, Mexicans, Venezuelans, Chileans, Taiwanese, Peruvians, Asian people, Uruguayans and the largest group of all; Argentines.[120][121][122] Along with German Argentines, German Paraguayans are one of the most prominent and growing German communities in South America, with some 25,000 German-speaking Mennonites living in the Paraguayan Chaco.[123][124] German settlers founded several towns, such as Hohenau, Filadelfia, Neuland, Obligado and Nueva Germania.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Several websites that promote German immigration to Paraguay claim that 5–7% of the population is of German ancestry,[dubious – discuss] including 150,000 people of German-Brazilian descent.[better source needed][125][126][127][128][129] Similarly, from the 1920–30s, Paraguay received waves of Slavic immigrants who settled in Asunción and Southern Paraguay (Itapúa, Misiones and Ñeembucú), especially in the towns of Fram, Coronel Bogado, Encarnación, San Juan del Paraná, San Ignacio, and Pilar.[130][131] Paraguay has also been a haven for communities persecuted for the religious faith, like the Bruderhof who were forced to leave England in 1941 because of their pacifist beliefs.[132][133] Many of these communities have retained their languages and culture, particularly the Brazilians, who represent one of the largest immigrant groups.[134] Many Brazilian Paraguayans are of German, Italian and Polish descent.[135] There are an estimated 8,000 Afro-Paraguayans, comprising 0.13% of the population.[citation needed]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Paraguay is a developing country, ranking 99th in the Human Development Index,[12] with the seventh highest GDP (PPP) per capita in South America.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>As of 2024, it had one of the fastest growing economies in the Western Hemisphere, driven by beef and soybean exports, manufacturing, and construction.[13] Paraguay is one of the world's leading exporters of hydroelectricity; the Itaipu Dam on the Paraná River border with Brazil is the third largest hydroelectric dam in the world in terms of produced energy.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Paraguay is a founding member of Mercosur, the United Nations, the Organization of American States, the Non-Aligned Movement and the Lima Group.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Additionally, the city of Luque, in metropolitan Asunción, is the seat of the South American Football Confederation.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Spanish and Guaraní are the two main languages in Paraguay, with both having official status.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The Guaraní language is a remarkable trace of the indigenous Guaraní culture that has endured in Paraguay.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Guaraní is one of the last commonly used indigenous national languages in South America.[137] In 2015, Spanish was spoken by about 87% of the population, while Guaraní is spoken by more than 90%, or slightly more than 5.8 million speakers.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Of rural Paraguayans, 52% are bilingual in Guaraní and Spanish.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>While Guaraní is still widely spoken, Spanish is generally given a preferential treatment in government, business, media and education as a South American lingua franca.[138][139][140][141]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>After Francia's death in 1840, Paraguay was ruled by various military officers under a new junta militar, until Carlos Antonio López (allegedly Rodríguez de Francia's nephew) came to power in 1841.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>López modernized Paraguay and opened it to foreign commerce.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>He signed a nonaggression pact with Argentina and officially declared independence of Paraguay in 1842.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After López's death in 1862, power was transferred to his eldest son, Francisco Solano López.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.text:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The official language is Hebrew.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Hebrew is the primary language of the state and is spoken daily by the majority of the population.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Prior to 1948, opposition to Yiddish, the historical language of the Ashkenazi Jews, was common among supporters of the Zionist movement, including the Yishuv, who sought to promote Hebrew's revival as a unifying national language.[637] These sentiments were reflected in the early policies of the Israeli government, which largely banned Yiddish theatre and publications.[638] Until 2018, Arabic was also an official language;[12] in 2018 it was downgraded to having a "special status in the state".[10][11] Arabic is spoken by the Arab minority, with Arabic and Hebrew taught in Arab schools.[639] Arabic is studied in most Jewish schools and is often used on signage and in transport announcements.[640]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Israel maintains diplomatic relations with 165 UN member states, the Holy See, Kosovo, the Cook Islands and Niue.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It has 107 diplomatic missions;[445] countries with which it has no diplomatic relations include most Muslim countries.[446] Six out of 22 nations in the Arab League have normalised relations with Israel.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Israel remains formally in a state of war with Syria, dating back uninterrupted to 1948.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It has been in a similarly formal state of war with Lebanon since the end of the Lebanese Civil War in 2000, with the Israel–Lebanon border remaining unagreed by treaty.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Although Turkey and Israel did not establish full diplomatic relations until 1991,[464] Turkey has cooperated with the Jewish state since its recognition of Israel in 1949.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Turkey's ties to other Muslim-majority nations in the region have at times resulted in pressure from Arab and Muslim states to temper its relationship with Israel.[465] Relations took a downturn after the 2008–09 Gaza War and Israel's raid of the Gaza flotilla.[466] Relations between Greece and Israel have improved since 1995 after decline of Israeli–Turkish relations.[467] The two countries have a defence cooperation agreement and in 2010, the Israeli Air Force hosted Greece's Hellenic Air Force in a joint exercise.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The joint Cyprus-Israel oil and gas explorations centered on the Leviathan gas field are an important factor for Greece, given its strong links with Cyprus.[468] Cooperation in the world's longest submarine power cable, the EuroAsia Interconnector, has strengthened Cyprus–Israel relations.[469]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Due to mass immigration from the former Soviet Union and Ethiopia (some 130,000 Ethiopian Jews live in Israel),[641][642] Russian and Amharic are widely spoken.[643] Over one million Russian-speaking immigrants arrived in Israel between 1990 and 2004.[644] French is spoken by around 700,000 Israelis,[645] mostly originating from France and North Africa (see Maghrebi Jews).<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>English was an official language during the Mandate period;[646] it lost this status after the establishment of Israel, but retains a role comparable to that of an official language.[647][648] Many Israelis communicate reasonably well in English, as many television programmes are broadcast in English with subtitles and the language is taught in elementary school.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Israeli universities offer courses in English.[649][better source needed]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Israel has no official religion,[355][356][357] but the definition of the state as "Jewish and democratic" creates a strong connection with Judaism.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>On 19 July 2018, the Knesset passed a Basic Law that characterises Israel as principally a "Nation State of the Jewish People" and Hebrew as its official language.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The bill ascribes an undefined "special status" to the Arabic language.[358] The same bill gives Jews a unique right to national self-determination and views the developing of Jewish settlement in the country as "a national interest", empowering the government to "take steps to encourage, advance and implement this interest".[359]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The United States and the Soviet Union were the first two countries to recognise the State of Israel, having declared recognition roughly simultaneously.[452] Diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union were broken in 1967 following the Six-Day War and renewed in 1991.[453] The United States regards Israel as its "most reliable partner in the Middle East",[454] based on "common democratic values, religious affinities, and security interests".[455] The US has provided $68 billion in military assistance and $32 billion in grants to Israel since 1967, under the Foreign Assistance Act (period beginning 1962),[456] more than any other country for that period until 2003.[456][457][458] Most surveyed Americans have held consistently favourable views of Israel.[459][460] The United Kingdom is seen as having a "natural" relationship with Israel because of the Mandate for Palestine.[461] By 2007[update], Germany had paid 25 billion euros in reparations to Israel and individual Israeli Holocaust survivors.[462] Israel is included in the European Union's European Neighbourhood Policy.[463]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Sri Lanka
entity_document.text:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Sinhala and Tamil are the two official languages.[327] The constitution defines English as the link language.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>English is widely used for education, scientific and commercial purposes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Members of the Burgher community speak variant forms of Portuguese Creole and Dutch with varying proficiency, while members of the Malay community speak a form of Creole Malay that is unique to the island.[328]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Sri Lanka,[a] officially the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, formerly known as Ceylon,[b] is an island country in South Asia.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is located in the Indian Ocean, southwest of the Bay of Bengal, and is separated from India by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Sri Lanka shares a maritime border with the Maldives to the southwest and India to the northwest, and lies across the Bay of Bengal from Bangladesh and Myanmar to the northeast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands of India to the east.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Its capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, while Colombo is its largest city and the political, financial and cultural centre. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Sri Lanka's population is 22 million; with the Sinhalese people, who speak the Sinhala language, forming the vast majority—while Tamil is spoken by the large Tamil minority.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Other long-established ethnic groups include the Moors, Indian Tamils, Burghers, Malays, Chinese, and Vedda.[15]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Sri Lanka is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>While ensuring that it maintains its independence, Sri Lanka has cultivated relations with India.[245] Sri Lanka became a member of the United Nations in 1955.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Today, it is also a member of the Commonwealth, the SAARC, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the Asian Development Bank, and the Colombo Plan.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike was elected prime minister in 1956. <<Q_RELEVANT>>His three-year rule had a profound influence through his self-proclaimed role of "defender of the besieged Sinhalese culture".[118] He introduced the controversial Sinhala Only Act, recognising Sinhala as the only official language of the government.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Although partially reversed in 1958, the bill posed a grave concern for the Tamil community, which perceived in it a threat to their language and culture.[119][120][121]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The Bandaranaike government of 1956 significantly changed the pro-western policies set by the previous UNP government. It recognised Cuba under Fidel Castro in 1959. <<A_RELEVANT>>Shortly afterward, Cuba's revolutionary Che Guevara paid a visit to Sri Lanka.[250] The Sirima-Shastri Pact of 1964[251] and Sirima-Gandhi Pact of 1974[252] were signed between Sri Lankan and Indian leaders in an attempt to solve the long-standing dispute over the status of plantation workers of Indian origin.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>In 1974, Kachchatheevu, a small island in Palk Strait, was formally ceded to Sri Lanka.[253] By this time, Sri Lanka was strongly involved in the NAM, and the fifth NAM summit was held in Colombo in 1976.[254] The relationship between Sri Lanka and India became tense under the government of J.<</QA_RELEVANT>> R. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Jayawardene.[140][255] To this end, Sri Lanka had briefly adopted a 'Look East' policy,[256]: 1  and at one point pursued ASEAN membership over joining SAARC.[257][258]: 64  Further deterioration led to the Indian intervention in the Sri Lankan Civil War and subsequently deployed an Indian Peace Keeping Force in 1987.[259] In the present, Sri Lanka enjoys extensive relations with China,[260] Russia,[261] and Pakistan.[262]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Executive: The President of Sri Lanka is the head of state; the commander in chief of the armed forces; chief executive, and is popularly elected for a five-year term.[203] The president heads the cabinet and appoints ministers from elected members of parliament.[204] The president is immune from legal proceedings while in the office with respect to any acts done or omitted to be done by him or her in either an official or private capacity.[205] Following the passage of the 19th amendment to the constitution in 2015, the president has two terms, which previously stood at no term limit.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In the 21st century, Sri Lanka has emerged as a developing country, with a strategically important geographical location in the Indian Ocean, with its deep harbors giving it significant geopolitical leverage as a major trading post from the ancient Maritime Silk Road.[20][21][22] It has the highest level of human development in South Asia and the second-highest GDP per capita in the region.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Sri Lanka has a long history of International engagement and cooperation, and is a member of several international organisations—including SAARC, the G77, the Non-Aligned Movement and the Commonwealth of Nations.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

question: This Asian island nation’s lowest point lies at sea level in the Indian Ocean, its official language is Maldivian (Dhivehi), and it is a member of the Commonwealth of Nations. Using 2021 data, calculate the country’s human‑capital proxy defined as life expectancy at birth × the percentage of the population attaining at least secondary education × log₁₀(GDP per capita). Report the result rounded to one decimal place.

entity_document.title: Maldives
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>Maldives is the smallest country in Asia.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its land area is only 298 square kilometres (115 sq mi), but this is spread over roughly 90,000 square kilometres (35,000 sq mi) of the sea, making it one of the world's most spatially dispersed sovereign states.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>With a population of 515,132 in the 2022 census, it is the second least populous country in Asia and the ninth-smallest country by area, but also one of the most densely populated countries.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Maldives has an average ground-level elevation of around 1.5 metres (4 ft 11 in) above sea level,[8] and a highest natural point of only 2.4 metres (7 ft 10 in), making it the world's lowest-lying country.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some sources state the highest point, Mount Villingili, as 5.1 metres or 17 feet.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Maldives is a presidential constitutional republic, with extensive influence of the president as head of government and head of state.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The president heads the executive branch and appoints the cabinet which is approved by the People's Majlis (Parliament).<</Q_RELEVANT>> He leads the armed forces. <<QA_RELEVANT>>The current president serving since 17 November 2023 is Mohamed Muizzu.[131][132] President of Maldives and Members of the unicameral Majlis serve five-year terms.[133] The total number of members are determined by atoll populations.<</QA_RELEVANT>> At the 2024 parliamentary election, the People's National Congress (PNC) won a super-majority over the 93 constituencies.[134]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Since 1996, Maldives has been the official progress monitor of the Indian Ocean Commission.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>In 2002, Maldives began to express interest in the commission but as of 2008[update] had not applied for membership.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Maldives' interest relates to its identity as a small island state, especially economic development and environmental preservation, and its desire for closer relations with France, a main actor in the IOC region.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Malé is the capital and the most populated city, traditionally called the "King's Island", where the ancient royal dynasties ruled from its central location.[9] Maldives has been inhabited for over 2,500 years.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Documented contact with the outside world began around 947 AD when Arab travellers began visiting the islands. <<QA_RELEVANT>>In the 12th century, partly due to the importance of the Arabs and Persians as traders in the Indian Ocean, Islam reached the Maldivian Archipelago.[10] Maldives was soon consolidated as a sultanate, developing strong commercial and cultural ties with Asia and Africa.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>From the mid-16th century, the region came under the increasing influence of European colonial powers, with Maldives becoming a British protectorate in 1887.<</A_RELEVANT>> Independence from the United Kingdom came in 1965, and a presidential republic was established in 1968 with an elected People's Majlis. <<QA_RELEVANT>>The ensuing decades have seen political instability, efforts at democratic reform,[11] and environmental challenges posed by climate change and rising sea levels.[12] Maldives became a founding member of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).<</QA_RELEVANT>>

As a water-bound nation, much of its security concerns life at sea. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Almost 99% of the country is covered by sea and the remaining 1% land is scattered over an area of 800 km (497 mi) × 120 km (75 mi), with the largest island being not more than 8 km2 (3 sq mi).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Therefore, the duties assigned to the MNDF of maintaining surveillance over Maldives' waters and providing protection against foreign intruders poaching in the EEZ and territorial waters, are immense tasks from both logistical and economic viewpoints.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The British expelled the Dutch from Ceylon in 1796 and included Maldives as a British protectorate.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The status of Maldives as a British protectorate was officially recorded in an 1887 agreement in which the sultan Muhammad Mueenuddeen II accepted British influence over Maldivian external relations and defence while retaining home rule, which continued to be regulated by Muslim traditional institutions in exchange for an annual tribute.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The status of the islands was akin to other British protectorates in the Indian Ocean region, including Zanzibar and the Trucial States.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Only near the southern end of this natural coral barricade do two open passages permit safe ship navigation from one side of the Indian Ocean to the other through the territorial waters of Maldives.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>For administrative purposes, the Maldivian government organised these atolls into 21 administrative divisions.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The largest island of Maldives is that of Gan, which belongs to Laamu Atoll or Hahdhummathi Maldives.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In Addu Atoll, the westernmost islands are connected by roads over the reef (collectively called Link Road), and the total length of the road is 14 km (9 mi).<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The PRC has diplomatic relations with 179 United Nations member-states and maintains embassies in 174.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>As of 2024[update], China has the largest diplomatic networks of any country in the world.[207] China is of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.[208] It is a member of intergovernmental organizations including the G20,[209] the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation,[210] the BRICS,[211] the East Asia Summit,[212] and the APEC.[213] China is also a former member and leader of the Non-Aligned Movement and still considers itself an advocate for developing countries.[214] China is widely described as either a potential or established superpower,[215][216][217] due to its influence in the fields of geopolitics, technology, manufacturing, economics and culture.[218][219][220]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Much of current Chinese foreign policy is officially based on Premier Zhou Enlai's Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, as well as by the concept of "harmony without uniformity", which encourages diplomatic relations between states despite ideological differences.[221] Per its policy of non-alignment, China maintains no military alliances except its defense treaty with North Korea.[222] Most countries have switched recognition from the ROC to the PRC since the latter replaced the former in the UN in 1971.[223] The PRC officially maintains the one China principle: the view that there is only one sovereign state with the name "China"—represented by the PRC—and that Taiwan is an integral part of China.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The unique status of Taiwan has led to countries formally recognizing the PRC to maintain unique "one China policies" that differ from each other; some countries explicitly recognize the PRC's claim over Taiwan, while others, including the U.S. and Japan, only acknowledge the claim.[224]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>China has a close political, economic and military relationship with Russia,[225] and the two states often vote in unison in the UN Security Council.[226][227] China has provided Russia with economic, technological, and diplomatic support during the Russo-Ukrainian war.[228][229] China's relationship with the United States is complex, and includes deep trade ties but significant political differences.[230] Since the early 2000s, China has followed a policy of engaging with African nations for trade and bilateral co-operation.[231][232][233] It maintains extensive and highly diversified trade links with the European Union, and became its largest trading partner for goods.[234] China is increasing its influence in Central Asia[235] and South Pacific.[236] The country has strong trade ties with ASEAN countries[237] and major South American economies,[238] and is the largest trading partner of Brazil, Chile, Peru, Uruguay, Argentina, and several others.[239]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>After Mao's death, the Gang of Four were arrested by Hua Guofeng.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The Cultural Revolution was rebuked, with millions rehabilitated. <<A_RELEVANT>>Deng Xiaoping took power in 1978, and started the reform and opening up, instituting large-scale political and economic reforms to transition away from planned economy.[112][113] China adopted its current constitution on 4 December 1982.[114] In 1989, there were protests such those in Tiananmen Square, and then throughout the entire nation.[115] Jiang Zemin was elevated to become the CCP general secretary, becoming the paramount leader.[116][117] China's economy grew sevenfold during Jiang's tenure.[118] British Hong Kong and Portuguese Macau returned to China in 1997 and 1999, respectively, as special administrative regions under the principle of one country, two systems.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>In 2002, Hu Jintao succeeded Jiang as the general secretary.[118] Under Hu, China maintained its high rate of economic growth, overtaking the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Japan to become the world's second-largest economy.[119] However, the growth also severely impacted the country's resources and environment,[120][121] and caused major social displacement.[122][123] Xi Jinping succeeded Hu as paramount leader in 2012.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Shortly after his ascension to power, Xi launched a vast anti-corruption crackdown,[124] that prosecuted more than 2 million officials by 2022.[125] During his tenure, Xi has consolidated power unseen since the initiation of economic and political reforms.[126]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Malaysia is tropical and is one of 17 megadiverse countries; it is home to numerous endemic species.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The country is multiethnic and multicultural, which has a significant effect on its politics.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>About half the population is ethnically Malay, with minorities of Chinese, Indians, and indigenous peoples.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The official language is Malaysian Malay, a standard form of the Malay language.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>English remains an active second language.<</Q_RELEVANT>> While recognising Islam as the official religion, the constitution grants freedom of religion to non-Muslims. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The government is modelled on the Westminster parliamentary system, and the legal system is based on common law.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The head of state is an elected monarch, chosen among the nine state rulers every five years.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The head of government is the prime minister.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Executive power is vested in the Cabinet, led by the Prime Minister. The prime minister must be a member of the House of Representatives, who in the opinion of His Majesty the King, commands the support of a majority of members. <<QA_RELEVANT>>The Cabinet is chosen from members of both houses of Parliament.[51] The Prime Minister is both the head of cabinet and the head of government.[83] As a result of the 2018 general election Malaysia was governed by the Pakatan Harapan (PH) political alliance,[77] although Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad resigned amid a political crisis in 2020.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>In March 2020, the Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition formed under Prime Minister Muhyiddin Yassin,[88] before Muhyiddin lost majority support and was replaced by deputy Prime Minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob, a veteran politician from the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), in August 2021.[89][90] As a result of the 2022 Malaysian general election, a hung parliament was elected.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Anwar Ibrahim of the PH coalition was appointed as the new Prime Minister to lead the coalition government of PH, Barisan Nasional, Gabungan Parti Sarawak, Gabungan Rakyat Sabah and several other political parties and independents.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Meanwhile, PN, the only political coalition not in the coalition government became the Opposition.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>English remains an active second language, with its use allowed for some official purposes under the National Language Act of 1967.[287] In Sarawak, English is an official state language alongside Malay.[288][289][290] Historically, English was the de facto administrative language; Malay became predominant after the 1969 race riots (13 May incident).[291] Malaysian English, also known as Malaysian Standard English, is a form of English derived from British English.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Malaysian English is widely used in business, along with Manglish, which is a colloquial form of English with heavy Malay, Chinese, and Tamil influences.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The government discourages the use of non-standard Malay but has no power to issue compounds or fines to those who use what is perceived as improper Malay on their advertisements.[292][293]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>There are also two other non-Bumiputera local ethnic groups. 22.8% of the population are Malaysian Chinese, while 6.8% are Malaysian Indian.[256] The local Chinese have historically been more dominant in the business community.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Local Indians are mostly of Tamil descent.[262][263] Malaysian citizenship is not automatically granted to those born in Malaysia, but is granted to a child born of two Malaysian parents outside Malaysia.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Dual citizenship is not permitted.[264] Citizenship in the states of Sabah and Sarawak in Malaysian Borneo are distinct from citizenship in Peninsular Malaysia for immigration purposes.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Every citizen is issued a biometric smart chip identity card known as MyKad at the age of 12 and must carry the card at all times.[265]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Positioned below the federal and state governments, local governments represent the lowest tier of governance in Malaysia.[108] As of 2024[update], Malaysia is divided between 19 cities, 40 municipalities, 91 district-level councils, and four statutory agencies.[112] While the federal constitution assigns local authorities to the exclusive jurisdiction of state governments,[113] in practice, the federal Ministry of Housing and Local Government oversees the regulation of local laws and policies.[108][114] Mayors (or presidents for municipal and district councils) and councillors are appointed by the respective state governments, or in the case of the federal territories, by the federal government.[115]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Malaysia is the world's 23rd-largest exporter and 25th-largest importer.[220][221] However, economic inequalities exist between different ethnic groups.[222] The Chinese make up about one-quarter of the population, but account for 70% of the country's market capitalisation.[223] Chinese businesses in Malaysia are part of the larger bamboo network, a network of overseas Chinese businesses in the Southeast Asian market sharing common family and cultural ties.[224]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Portugal, officially the Portuguese Republic, is a country located on the Iberian Peninsula in Southwestern Europe.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It is a unitary republic made up by mainland Portugal and two autonomous regions, with Lisbon as both its capital and largest city.<</QA_RELEVANT>> It has a total population of over 10.7 million. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The mainland borders Spain to the north and east, with Madeira and the Azores in the Atlantic Ocean.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It features the westernmost point in continental Europe.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>A member state of the United Nations since 1955,[107] Portugal is a founding member of NATO (1949),[174] the OECD (1961)[175] and EFTA (1960);[108] it left the last in 1986 to join the European Economic Community, which became the European Union in 1993.[122] In 1996, Portugal co-founded the Community of Portuguese Language Countries (CPLP), an international organisation and political association of Lusophone nations where Portuguese is an official language.[176]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>A developed country, Portugal has an advanced economy relying chiefly upon services, industry, and tourism.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Shaped by the various civilisations that have crossed its territory, it has developed a specific culture with a vast influence that allowed Portuguese to become the world's fifth-most spoken native language with more than 250 million native speakers.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Portugal is a member of the United Nations, European Union, Schengen Area, and Council of Europe, and one of the founding members of NATO, the eurozone, the OECD, and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Assembly of the Republic is an unicameral parliament composed of a maximum of 230 deputies elected for a four-year term.[165] The government is headed by the prime minister and includes ministers and secretaries of state, that have full executive powers;[166] the current prime minister is Luís Montenegro.[167] The Council of Ministers – under the prime minister[t] and the ministers – acts as the cabinet.[168] The courts are organised into several levels, among the judicial, administrative and fiscal branches.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The supreme courts are institutions of last appeal. The Constitutional Court oversees the constitutionality of the laws.[169]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The head of state is the president, elected to a five-year term by direct, universal suffrage, the incumbent is António José Seguro.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Although largely a ceremonial post,[162] presidential powers include the appointment of the prime minister and other members of the government, dismissing the prime minister, dissolving the parliament, vetoing legislation[r] and declaring war.[s][163] The president has also supervisory and reserve powers and is the ex officio supreme commander of the armed forces.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The president is advised on issues of importance by the Council of State.[164]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Portuguese is the official language of Portugal.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Mirandese is also recognised as a co-official regional language in some municipalities of North-Eastern Portugal.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It is part of the Astur-Leonese group of languages.[310] An estimate of between 6,000 and 7,000 Mirandese speakers has been documented for Portugal.[311] Furthermore, a particular dialect known as Barranquenho, spoken in Barrancos, is also officially recognised and protected in Portugal since 2021.[312] Minderico, a sociolect of the Portuguese language, is spoken by around 500 people in the town of Minde.[313]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Portugal remained neutral in World War II.[106] From the 1940s to 1960s, Portugal was a founding member of NATO, OECD, and EFTA, it also joined the United Nations in 1955.[107][108] New economic development projects and relocation of mainland Portuguese citizens into the overseas provinces in Africa were initiated, with Angola and Mozambique being the main destinations.[m][109] However, indigenous peoples were second-class citizens and sidelined on those development projects,[110] which led to the emergence of independence movements in Angola,[111] Mozambique, and Guinea in the 1960s, culminating in 1961 in the Portuguese Colonial War, which lasted until 1974.[112]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Portugal has hosted several international summits and events like the first EU–Brazil summit in July 2007, the second EU–African Union summit in December 2007, the signing of the Treaty of Lisbon also in December 2007, and the NATO summit in November 2010.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Portugal was a full member of the Latin Union (1983)[177] and the Organisation of Ibero-American States (1949).[178] It has a friendship alliance and dual citizenship treaty with Brazil.[179] Portugal and the United Kingdom share the world's oldest active military accord through their Anglo-Portuguese Alliance, signed in 1386.[60]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Kazakhstan is officially a bilingual country.[253] Kazakh (part of the Kipchak sub-branch of the Turkic languages)[254] was proficiently spoken by 80.1% of the population according to 2021 census,[255]: 323  and has the status of "state language".<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Russian, on the other hand, was spoken by 83.7% as of 2021.[256] It has equal status to Kazakh as an "official language", and is used routinely in business, government, and inter-ethnic communication.[257] However, only 63.4% of ethnic Kazakhs and 49.3% of the country's population are daily speakers of the Kazakh language, according to the same census.[255]: 382<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Each region is headed by an äkim (regional governor) appointed by the president.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>District äkimi are appointed by regional äkims.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>On 10 December 1997, Kazakhstan's government relocated its capital from Almaty, established under the Soviet Union, to Astana.[113]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Kazakhstan has a bicameral parliament composed of the Majilis (the lower house) and senate (the upper house).[97] Single-mandate districts popularly elect 107 seats in the Majilis; there also are ten members elected by party-list vote.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The senate has 48 members.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Two senators are selected by each of the elected assemblies (mäslihats) of Kazakhstan's twenty principal administrative divisions (seventeen regions and three nationally significant cities).[98] The president appoints the remaining fifteen senators.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Majilis deputies and the government both have the right of legislative initiative, though the government proposes most legislation considered by the parliament.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Following the collapse of central government in Petrograd in November 1917, the Kazakhs (then in Russia officially referred to as "Kirghiz") experienced a brief period of autonomy (the Alash Autonomy) before eventually succumbing to the Bolsheviks' rule.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>On 26 August 1920, the Kirghiz Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR) was established.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The Kirghiz ASSR included the territory of present-day Kazakhstan, but its administrative centre was the mainly Russian-populated town of Orenburg.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 1925, the Kirghiz ASSR was renamed the Kazak ASSR and its administrative centre was transferred to the town of Kyzylorda, and in April 1927 to Alma-Ata.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Despite their traditionally nomadic lifestyle, the Kazakhs were among the most literate groups in Central Asia, which set them apart in the region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, Soviet policies, including forced collectivization and repression of the traditional elite in the late 1920s and 1930s, led to devastating consequences for the Kazakh population.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>These policies caused widespread famine and high fatalities, with an estimated 1.5 million deaths between 1926 and 1939, mostly due to starvation and related diseases, as well as violence (see also: Famine in Kazakhstan of 1932–33).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Thousands of Kazakhs fled to China, but many did not survive the journey.[44][56][57] During the 1930s, some members of the Kazakh intelligentsia were executed – as part of the policies of political reprisals pursued by the Soviet government in Moscow.[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Russian Empire introduced an administrative system and built military garrisons and barracks in its effort to establish a presence in Central Asia in the so-called "Great Game" for dominance in the area against the British Empire, which was extending its influence from the south in India and Southeast Asia.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Russia built its first outpost, Orsk, in 1735. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Russia introduced the Russian language in all schools and governmental organizations.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Russia's efforts to impose its system aroused the resentment of the Kazakhs, and, by the 1860s, some Kazakhs resisted its rule.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Russia had disrupted the traditional nomadic lifestyle and livestock-based economy, and people were suffering from starvation, with some Kazakh tribes being decimated.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Kazakh national movement, which began in the late 19th century, sought to preserve the native language and identity by resisting the attempts of the Russian Empire to assimilate and stifle Kazakh culture.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Officially, Kazakhstan is a democratic, secular, constitutional unitary republic; Nursultan Nazarbayev led the country from 1991 to 2019.[92][93] He was succeeded by Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.[94][95] The president may veto legislation that has been passed by the parliament and is also the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The prime minister chairs the cabinet of ministers and serves as Kazakhstan's head of government.<</QA_RELEVANT>> There are three deputy prime ministers and sixteen ministers in the cabinet.[96]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932 by King Abdulaziz, who united Hejaz, Najd, parts of Eastern Arabia and South Arabia (Asir) into a single state through a series of military and political campaigns beginning in 1901.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The country has since been governed as an absolute monarchy under the House of Saud.[24] In its Basic Law, Saudi Arabia defines itself as a sovereign Arab Islamic state with Islam as its official religion and Arabic as its official language.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The ultraconservative Wahhabi religious movement within Sunni Islam was the prevailing political and cultural force until the 2000s.[25][26] The Saudi government has attracted criticism for various policies such as its intervention in the Yemeni Civil War, restrictions on political and civil liberties, and poor human rights record.[27][28][29] Since the mid-2010s, Saudi Arabia has instituted limited and gradual reforms to liberalize social, cultural, and religious life.[30]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Relations with the U.S. became strained following 9/11 terror attacks.[258] American politicians and media accused the Saudi government of supporting terrorism and tolerating a jihadist culture.[259] According to former U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in December 2010, "Saudi Arabia remains a critical financial support base for al-Qaida, the Taliban, LeT and other terrorist groups...<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Donors in Saudi Arabia constitute the most significant source of funding to Sunni terrorist groups worldwide."[260] The Saudi government denies these claims or that it exports religious or cultural extremism.[261] In September 2016, the U.S.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act that would allow relatives of victims of the 11 September attacks to sue Saudi Arabia for its government's alleged role in the attacks.[262] In 2014, Sheikh Abdulaziz bin Abdullah Al-Sheikh, the Grand Mufti of Saudi Arabia and Chairman of the Council of Senior Scholars, issued a fatwa explicitly prohibiting joining or supporting terrorist organizations such as ISIS and al-Qaeda.[263] According to the U.S.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Department of State, "Saudi Arabia plays an important role in working toward a peaceful and prosperous future for the region and is a strong partner in security and counterterrorism efforts and in military, diplomatic, and financial cooperation."[264] A significant Saudi counterterrorism success was the foiling of a 2010 cargo plane bomb plot.[265] In December 2015, Saudi Arabia announced the formation of the Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition, an alliance of Muslim-majority countries aimed at combating terrorism and extremism.[266]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

Historically, Saudi women have faced discrimination in many aspects of their lives and were effectively treated as legal minors under the male guardianship system.[310] The treatment of women has been referred to as "sex segregation"[311][312] and "gender apartheid".[313][314] Since the 2000s, the kingdom has made several attempts to improve the status of women in order to elevate their global standing. As of June 2023, the kingdom has reportedly reversed its ban on women "becoming lawyers, engineers, or geologists" and established "aggressive affirmative action programmes", doubling the female labour force participation rate. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It has added "its first female newspaper editors, diplomats, TV anchors and public prosecutors", with a female head of the Saudi stock exchange and member on the board of Saudi Aramco.[315] In June 2018, the Saudi government issued a law allowing women to drive.[316] However, an investigation by The Guardian newspaper in 2025 found that the Dar al-Reaya, officially "care homes", continued to be effectively "jails" for women whose families wished to institutionalize them for disobedience, extramarital sexual relations or being absent from home.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Some women are sent to Dar al-Reaya to protect a family's reputation after a woman is sexually abused by a brother or father. Treatment was reported to be "hellish": with solitary confinement, flogging, and no family contact.[317]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The foreign policy of Saudi Arabia is officially focused on cooperation with the oil-exporting Gulf States, the unity of the Arab world, Islamic solidarity, and support for the United Nations and multilateralism.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It joined the UN in 1945[44][226] and is a founding member of the Arab League, Gulf Cooperation Council, Muslim World League, and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.[f][227] Saudi Arabia joined the World Trade Organization in 2005 and plays a prominent role in the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the G20.[44] Although part of the Non-Aligned Movement, Saudi Arabia is generally considered pro-Western.[228]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Relations with the U.S. became strained following 9/11 terror attacks.[258] American politicians and media accused the Saudi government of supporting terrorism and tolerating a jihadist culture.[259] According to former U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in December 2010, "Saudi Arabia remains a critical financial support base for al-Qaida, the Taliban, LeT and other terrorist groups...<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Donors in Saudi Arabia constitute the most significant source of funding to Sunni terrorist groups worldwide."[260] The Saudi government denies these claims or that it exports religious or cultural extremism.[261] In September 2016, the U.S.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act that would allow relatives of victims of the 11 September attacks to sue Saudi Arabia for its government's alleged role in the attacks.[262] In 2014, Sheikh Abdulaziz bin Abdullah Al-Sheikh, the Grand Mufti of Saudi Arabia and Chairman of the Council of Senior Scholars, issued a fatwa explicitly prohibiting joining or supporting terrorist organizations such as ISIS and al-Qaeda.[263] According to the U.S.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Department of State, "Saudi Arabia plays an important role in working toward a peaceful and prosperous future for the region and is a strong partner in security and counterterrorism efforts and in military, diplomatic, and financial cooperation."[264] A significant Saudi counterterrorism success was the foiling of a 2010 cargo plane bomb plot.[265] In December 2015, Saudi Arabia announced the formation of the Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition, an alliance of Muslim-majority countries aimed at combating terrorism and extremism.[266]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

Historically, Saudi women have faced discrimination in many aspects of their lives and were effectively treated as legal minors under the male guardianship system.[310] The treatment of women has been referred to as "sex segregation"[311][312] and "gender apartheid".[313][314] Since the 2000s, the kingdom has made several attempts to improve the status of women in order to elevate their global standing. As of June 2023, the kingdom has reportedly reversed its ban on women "becoming lawyers, engineers, or geologists" and established "aggressive affirmative action programmes", doubling the female labour force participation rate. <<Q_RELEVANT>>It has added "its first female newspaper editors, diplomats, TV anchors and public prosecutors", with a female head of the Saudi stock exchange and member on the board of Saudi Aramco.[315] In June 2018, the Saudi government issued a law allowing women to drive.[316] However, an investigation by The Guardian newspaper in 2025 found that the Dar al-Reaya, officially "care homes", continued to be effectively "jails" for women whose families wished to institutionalize them for disobedience, extramarital sexual relations or being absent from home.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Some women are sent to Dar al-Reaya to protect a family's reputation after a woman is sexually abused by a brother or father. Treatment was reported to be "hellish": with solitary confinement, flogging, and no family contact.[317]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The foreign policy of Saudi Arabia is officially focused on cooperation with the oil-exporting Gulf States, the unity of the Arab world, Islamic solidarity, and support for the United Nations and multilateralism.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It joined the UN in 1945[44][226] and is a founding member of the Arab League, Gulf Cooperation Council, Muslim World League, and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.[f][227] Saudi Arabia joined the World Trade Organization in 2005 and plays a prominent role in the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the G20.[44] Although part of the Non-Aligned Movement, Saudi Arabia is generally considered pro-Western.[228]<</QA_RELEVANT>>
