entity_document.title: France
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>France,[h] officially the French Republic,[i] is a country primarily located in Western Europe.[j] Its overseas regions and territories include French Guiana in South America, Saint Pierre and Miquelon in the North Atlantic in North America, the French West Indies, and many islands in Oceania and the Indian Ocean.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Metropolitan France shares borders with Belgium and Luxembourg to the north; Germany to the northeast; Switzerland to the east; Italy and Monaco to the southeast; Andorra and Spain to the south; and a maritime border with the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland to the northwest.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its metropolitan area extends from the Rhine to the Atlantic Ocean and from the Mediterranean Sea to the English Channel and the North Sea.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Its 18 integral regions—five of which are overseas—span a combined area of 632,702 km2 (244,288 sq mi), with a total population estimated at 69.1 million in 2026. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its capital, largest city and main cultural and economic centre is Paris.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The executive branch has two leaders.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The president, who is Emmanuel Macron since 2017, is the head of state, elected directly by universal adult suffrage for a five-year term.[114] The prime minister, who is Sébastien Lecornu since 2025, is the head of government, appointed by the president to lead the government.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The president has the power to dissolve parliament or circumvent it by submitting referendums directly to the people; the president also appoints judges and civil servants, negotiates and ratifies international agreements, and serves as commander-in-chief of the French Armed Forces. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The prime minister determines public policy and oversees the civil service, with an emphasis on domestic matters.[115] In the 2022 presidential election, Macron was re-elected.[116] Two months later in the legislative elections, Macron lost his parliamentary majority and had to form a minority government.[117]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>A new constitution resulted in the Fourth Republic (1946–1958), which saw strong economic growth (les Trente Glorieuses).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>France was a founding member of NATO and attempted to regain control of French Indochina, but was defeated by the Viet Minh in 1954.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>France faced another anti-colonialist conflict in Algeria, then part of France and home to over one million European settlers (Pied-Noir).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The French systematically used torture and repression, including extrajudicial killings to keep control.[66] This conflict nearly led to a coup and civil war.[67]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>French law is divided into two principal areas: private law and public law.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Private law includes, in particular, civil law and criminal law. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Public law includes, in particular, administrative law and constitutional law.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, in practical terms, French law comprises three principal areas of law: civil law, criminal law, and administrative law.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Criminal laws can only address the future and not the past (criminal ex post facto laws are prohibited).[163] While administrative law is often a subcategory of civil law in many countries, it is completely separated in France and each body of law is headed by a specific supreme court: ordinary courts (which handle criminal and civil litigation) are headed by the Court of Cassation and administrative courts are headed by the Council of State.<</QA_RELEVANT>> To be applicable, every law must be officially published in the Journal officiel de la République française.

The Franks embraced the Christian Gallo-Roman culture, and Gaul was renamed Francia ("Land of the Franks"). <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Germanic Franks adopted Romanic languages.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Clovis made Paris his capital and established the Merovingian dynasty, but his kingdom would not survive his death.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Franks treated land as a private possession and divided it among their heirs, so four kingdoms emerged from that of Clovis: Paris, Orléans, Soissons, and Rheims.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The last Merovingian kings lost power to their mayors of the palace (head of household).<</Q_RELEVANT>> One mayor of the palace, Charles Martel, defeated an Umayyad invasion at the Battle of Tours in 732.[33] His son, Pepin the Short, seized the crown of Francia from the weakened Merovingians and founded the Carolingian dynasty. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Pepin's son Charlemagne reunited the Frankish kingdoms and built an empire across Western and Central Europe.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>France has a social market economy characterised by sizeable government involvement and diversified sectors.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>For two centuries, it has consistently ranked among the ten largest globally; as of 2025[update] it is the world's ninth largest by purchasing power parity and second largest in the EU, after Germany.[173] Considered a great power with considerable economic strength,[174] it is a member of the Group of Seven leading industrialised countries, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and the G20.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>France ranked 13th in the 2025 Global Innovation Index.[175][176]<</A_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Samoa
entity_document.text:
<<A_RELEVANT>>The Lapita people discovered and settled the Samoan Islands around 3,500 years ago.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>They developed a Samoan language and Samoan cultural identity.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Because of the Samoans' seafaring skills, pre-20th-century European explorers referred to the entire island group, including American Samoa, as the "Navigator Islands".[14][15] The country became a colony of the German Empire in 1899 after the Tripartite Convention, and was known as German Samoa.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>German administration ended in August 1914 after New Zealand troops bloodlessly occupied the colony at the start of World War I.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>New Zealand officially gained control of the region as a League of Nations mandate in 1920, when it became the Territory of Western Samoa.[16] After being converted into a United Nations Trust Territory in 1946, Western Samoa gained independence on 1 January 1962 and officially returned to its original pre-occupation name Samoa on 4 July 1997.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Samoan (Gagana Fa'asāmoa) and English are the official languages.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Including second-language speakers, there are more speakers of Samoan than English in Samoa.[131] Samoan Sign Language is also commonly used among the deaf population of Samoa.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>To emphasise the importance of full inclusion with sign language, elementary Samoan Sign Language was taught to members of the Samoa Police Service, Red Cross Society, and public during the 2017 International Week of the Deaf.[132]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>From independence in 1962, the country was officially known as the Independent State of Western Samoa,[d] commonly known as Western Samoa.[e] From 4 July 1997, the country changed its name to Samoa, drawing protests from nearby American Samoa, although the former name remains in use, especially their .ws top-domain.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Samoa,[b] officially the Independent State of Samoa,[c] is an island country in Polynesia, part of Oceania, in the South Pacific Ocean.<</QA_RELEVANT>> It consists of two main islands (Savai'i and Upolu), two smaller, inhabited islands (Manono and Apolima), and several smaller, uninhabited islands, including the Aleipata Islands (Nuʻutele, Nuʻulua, Fanuatapu and Namua). <<A_RELEVANT>>Samoa is located 64 km (40 mi; 35 nmi) west of American Samoa, 889 km (552 mi; 480 nmi) northeast of Tonga, 1,152 km (716 mi; 622 nmi) northeast of Fiji, 483 km (300 mi; 261 nmi) east of Wallis and Futuna, 1,151 km (715 mi; 621 nmi) southeast of Tuvalu, 519 km (322 mi; 280 nmi) south of Tokelau, 4,190 km (2,600 mi; 2,260 nmi) southwest of Hawaii, and 610 km (380 mi; 330 nmi) northwest of Niue.<</A_RELEVANT>> The capital and largest city is Apia.

<<QA_RELEVANT>>On 4 July 1997 the government amended the constitution to change the name of the country from Western Samoa to Samoa,[64] the name it had been called by in the United Nations since it joined.[65] American Samoa protested against the name change, asserting that it diminished its own identity.[65]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Samoa is a unitary parliamentary democracy with 11 administrative divisions.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It was admitted to the United Nations on 15 December 1976[17] and the country is also a member of the Commonwealth of Nations, Non-Aligned Movement and the Pacific Islands Forum.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The island's defence is responsible to the New Zealand Defence Force.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>After repeated efforts by the Samoan independence movement, the New Zealand Western Samoa Act of 24 November 1961 terminated the Trusteeship Agreement and granted the country independence as the Independent State of Western Samoa, effective 1 January 1962.[56][57] Western Samoa, the first small-island country in the Pacific to become independent, signed a Treaty of Friendship with New Zealand later in 1962.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Western Samoa joined the Commonwealth of Nations on 28 August 1970.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>While independence was achieved at the beginning of January, Samoa annually celebrates 1 June as its independence day.[58][59]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Samoa may come from Samoan: Sāmoa, lit. 'holy centre', uniting a compound of Samoan: sā, lit. 'sacred' and Samoan: moa, lit. 'middle'.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The name is alternatively derived from a local chieftain named Samoa or an indigenous word meaning 'place of the moa', a now-extinct bird,[18][19] though the bird was known only from New Zealand.[20]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>From the end of World War I until 1962, New Zealand controlled Western Samoa as a Class C Mandate under trusteeship through the League of Nations,[36][41] then through the United Nations.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Between 1919 and 1962, Samoa was administered by the Department of External Affairs, a government department which had been specially created to oversee New Zealand's Island Territories and Samoa.[42] In 1943, this department was renamed the Department of Island Territories after a separate Department of External Affairs was created to conduct New Zealand's foreign affairs.[43] During the period of New Zealand control, their administrators were responsible for two major incidents.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Kemakeza remained in office until April 2006, when he lost the 2006 Solomon Islands general election and Snyder Rini became PM.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, allegations that Rini had used bribes from Chinese businessmen to buy the votes of members of Parliament led to mass rioting in the capital Honiara, concentrated on the city's Chinatown area.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Resentment against the minority Chinese business community led to much of Chinatown in the city being destroyed.[92] China sent chartered aircraft to evacuate Chinese out of the riots.[93] Evacuation of Australian and British citizens was on a much smaller scale.[94] Additional Australian, New Zealand, and Fijian police and troops were dispatched to try to quell the unrest. Rini eventually resigned before facing a motion of no-confidence in Parliament, and Parliament elected Manasseh Sogavare as prime minister.[95][96]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Solomon Islands is a member of the United Nations, Interpol, Commonwealth of Nations, Pacific Islands Forum, Pacific Community, International Monetary Fund, and the African, Caribbean, and Pacific (ACP) countries (Lomé Convention).<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Solomons were first settled by people coming from the Bismarck Islands and New Guinea during the Pleistocene era c. 30,000–28,000 BC, based on archaeological evidence found at Kilu Cave on Buka Island in the Autonomous Region of Bougainville, Papua New Guinea.[18][19] At this point sea levels were lower and Buka and Bougainville were physically joined to the southern Solomons in one landmass ("Greater Bougainville"), though it is unclear precisely how far south these early settlers spread as no other archaeological sites from this period have been found.[18] As sea levels rose as the Ice Age ended c. 4000–3500 BC, the Greater Bougainville landmass split into the numerous islands that exist today.[18][20] Evidence of later human settlements dating to c. 4500–2500 BC have been found at Poha Cave and Vatuluma Posovi Cave on Guadalcanal.[18] The ethnic identity of these early peoples is unclear, though it is thought that the speakers of the Central Solomon languages (a self-contained language family unrelated to other languages spoken in the Solomons) likely represent the descendants of these earlier settlers.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>From c. 1200–800 BC, Austronesian Lapita people began arriving from the Bismarcks with their characteristic ceramics.[18][21] Evidence for their presence has been found across the Solomon archipelago, as well at the Santa Cruz Islands in the south-east, with different islands being settled at different times.[18] Linguistic and genetic evidence suggests that the Lapita people "leap-frogged" the already inhabited main Solomon Islands and settled first on the Santa Cruz group, with later back-migrations bringing their culture to the main group.[22][23]  These peoples mixed with the native Solomon Islanders and over time their languages became dominant, with most of the 60–70 languages spoken there belonging to the Oceanic branch of the Austronesian language family.[24] Then, as now, communities tended to exist in small villages practising subsistence agriculture, though extensive inter-island trade networks existed.[18] Numerous ancient burial sites and other evidence of permanent settlements have been found from the period AD 1000–1500 throughout the islands, one of the most prominent examples being the Roviana cultural complex centred on the islands off the southern coast of New Georgia, where a large number of megalithic shrines and other structures were constructed in the 13th century.[25] The people of Solomon Islands were notorious for headhunting and cannibalism before the arrival of the Europeans.[26][27]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

In April 1896, colonial official Charles Morris Woodford was appointed as the British Acting Deputy Commissioner, and he was confirmed in his position in the following year. <<A_RELEVANT>>The Colonial Office appointed Woodford as the Resident Commissioner in the Solomon Islands on 17 February 1897.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He was directed to control the coercive labour recruitment practices, known as blackbirding, operating in the Solomon Island waters and to stop the illegal trade in firearms.[12][45] Woodford set up an administrative headquarters on the small island of Tulagi, having proclaimed it the protectorate capital in 1896.[46] and in 1898 and 1899 the Rennell and Bellona Islands, Sikaiana, the Santa Cruz Islands and outlying islands such as Anuta, Fataka, Temotu and Tikopia were added to the protectorate.[45][47] In 1900, under the terms of the Tripartite Convention of 1899, Germany ceded the Northern Solomon to Britain, minus Buka and Bougainville, the latter becoming part of German New Guinea despite geographically belonging to the Solomons archipelago.[39] This was when the Shortlands, Choiseul, Santa Isabel and Ontong Java became part of the Solomons.[46]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: The first country is a member of the African Union, participates in the Commonwealth of Nations, and lies off the east coast of Africa. The second country is also a member of the African Union, has Islam as its official religion, and is located in East Africa. Using 2022 data, what is the ratio of the second country's total population to the first country's total population?

entity_document.title: Comoros
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Comoros,[a] officially the Union of the Comoros,[b] is an archipelagic country made up of three islands in Southeastern Africa, located at the northern end of the Mozambique Channel in the Indian Ocean.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Its capital and largest city is Moroni. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The religion of the majority of the population - and the official state religion - is Islam.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Comoros proclaimed its independence from France on 6 July 1975.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The Comoros is the only country of the Arab League which is entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is a member state of the African Union, the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, and the Indian Ocean Commission.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The country has three official languages: Comorian, French and Arabic.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The islands of the Comoros Archipelago were formed by volcanic activity.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Mount Karthala, an active shield volcano located on Ngazidja, is the country's highest point, at 2,361 metres (7,746 feet).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It contains the Comoros' largest patch of disappearing rainforest.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Karthala is currently one of the most active volcanoes in the world, with a minor eruption in May 2006, and prior eruptions as recently as April 2005 and 1991. In the 2005 eruption, which lasted from 17 to 19 April, 40,000 citizens were evacuated, and the crater lake in the volcano's three-by-four-kilometre (2-by-2+1⁄2-mile) caldera was destroyed.[citation needed]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Comoros is formed by Ngazidja (Grande Comore), Mwali (Mohéli) and Ndzwani (Anjouan), three major islands in the Comoros Archipelago, as well as many minor islets.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The islands are officially known by their Comorian-language names, though international sources still use their French names (given in parentheses above).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The capital and largest city, Moroni, is located on Ngazidja and the most densely populated city is Anjouan.[63] The archipelago is situated in the Indian Ocean, in the Mozambique Channel, between the African coast (nearest to Mozambique and Tanzania) and Madagascar, with no land borders.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Arabic and French are also official languages, along with Comorian.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Arabic is widely known as a second language, being the language of Quranic teaching.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>French is the administrative language and the language of most non-Quranic formal education.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The most common languages in the Comoros are the Comorian languages, collectively known as Shikomori.<</QA_RELEVANT>> They are related to Swahili, and the four different variants (Shingazidja, Shimwali, Shindzwani and Shimaore) are spoken on each of the four islands. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Arabic and Latin scripts are both used, Arabic being the more widely used, and an official orthography has recently been developed for the Latin script.[109]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Comoros is a member of the United Nations, the African Union, the Arab League, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the Indian Ocean Commission and the African Development Bank.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>On 10 April 2008, the Comoros became the 179th nation to accept the Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.[79] The Comoros signed the UN treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.[80] Azali Assoumani, President of the Comoros and Chair of the African Union, attended the 2023 Russia–Africa Summit in Saint Petersburg.[81]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Comorian legal system rests on Islamic law, an inherited French (Napoleonic Code) legal code, and customary law (mila na ntsi).<</Q_RELEVANT>> Village elders, kadis or civilian courts settle most disputes. The judiciary is independent of the legislative and the executive. The Supreme Court acts as a Constitutional Council in resolving constitutional questions and supervising presidential elections. <<Q_RELEVANT>>As High Court of Justice, the Supreme Court also arbitrates in cases where the government is accused of malpractice.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Supreme Court consists of two members selected by the president, two elected by the Federal Assembly, and one by the council of each island.[73]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In November 1975, the Comoros became the 143rd member of the United Nations.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The new nation was defined as comprising the entire archipelago, although the citizens of Mayotte chose to become French citizens and keep their island as a French territory.[76]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Brazil
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>The official language of Brazil is Portuguese (Article 13 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Brazil), which almost all of the population speaks and is virtually the only language used in newspapers, radio, television, and for business and administrative purposes.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking nation in the Americas, making the language an important part of Brazilian national identity and giving it a national culture distinct from those of its Spanish-speaking neighbors.[421]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Brazil's international relations are based on Article 4 of the Federal Constitution, which establishes non-intervention, self-determination, international cooperation and the peaceful settlement of conflicts as the guiding principles of Brazil's relationship with other countries and multilateral organizations.[248] According to the Constitution, the President has ultimate authority over foreign policy, while Congress is tasked with reviewing and considering all diplomatic nominations and international treaties, as well as legislation relating to Brazilian foreign policy.[249]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Before the arrival of the Europeans, the boundaries between these groups and their subgroups were marked by wars that arose from differences in culture, language and moral beliefs.[53] These wars also involved large-scale military actions on land and water, with cannibalistic rituals on prisoners of war.[54][55] While heredity had some weight, leadership was a status more won over time than assigned in succession ceremonies and conventions.[53] Slavery among the indigenous groups had a different meaning than it had for Europeans, since it originated from a diverse socioeconomic organization, in which asymmetries were translated into kinship relations.[56]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Brazil,[c] officially the Federative Republic of Brazil,[d] is the largest country in South America.<</A_RELEVANT>> It is also the world's fifth-largest country by area and the seventh-largest by population, with over 213 million people. The country is a federation composed of 26 states and a Federal District, which hosts the capital, Brasília. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its most populous city is São Paulo, followed by Rio de Janeiro.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Brazil has the most Portuguese speakers in the world and is the only country in the Americas where Portuguese is an official language.[17][18]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>During the 1990s, Brazil saw a surge of critical and commercial success with films such as O Quatrilho (Fábio Barreto, 1995), O Que É Isso, Companheiro? (Bruno Barreto, 1997) and Central do Brasil (Walter Salles, 1998), all of which were nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, the latter receiving a Best Actress nomination for Fernanda Montenegro.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The 2002 crime film City of God, directed by Fernando Meirelles, was critically acclaimed, scoring 90% on Rotten Tomatoes,[515] being placed in Roger Ebert's Best Films of the Decade list[516] and receiving four Academy Award nominations in 2004, including Best Director. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Notable film festivals in Brazil include the São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro International Film Festivals and the Gramado Festival.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Bounded by the Atlantic Ocean on the east, Brazil has a coastline of 7,491 kilometers (4,655 mi).[19] Covering roughly half of South America's land area, it borders all other countries and territories on the continent except Ecuador and Chile.[20] Brazil encompasses a wide range of tropical and subtropical landscapes, as well as wetlands, savannas, plateaus, and low mountains.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It contains most of the Amazon basin, including the world's largest river system and most extensive virgin tropical forest.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Brazil has diverse wildlife, a variety of ecological systems, and extensive natural resources spanning numerous protected habitats.[19] The country ranks first among 17 megadiverse countries, with its natural heritage being the subject of significant global interest, as environmental degradation (through processes such as deforestation) directly affect global issues such as climate change and biodiversity loss.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Brazil is a regional and middle power,[22][23][24] and has been described as a rising global power.[25][26][27][28] It is an emerging,[29][30] upper-middle income economy and newly industrialized country,[31] with one of the 10 largest economies in the world in both nominal and PPP terms,[32][33] the largest economy in Latin America and the Southern Hemisphere, and the largest share of wealth in South America.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>With a complex and highly diversified economy, Brazil is one of the world's major or primary exporters of various agricultural goods, mineral resources, and manufactured products.[34] The country ranks thirteenth in the world by number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.[35] Brazil is a founding member of the United Nations, the G20, BRICS, G4, Mercosur, Organization of American States, Organization of Ibero-American States, and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries; it is also an observer state of the Arab League and a major non-NATO ally of the United States.[36][37]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Mali
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>In January 2022, due to deteriorating relations between Mali and the French government, the Mali government announced making Bambara the official language.[181] In July 2023, French was dropped as an official language, becoming instead a working language.[2] At the same time, the 13 national languages,[3] namely Bambara, Bobo, Bozo, Dogon, Fula, Hassaniya Arabic, Kassonke, Maninke, Minyanka, Senufo, the Songhai, Soninke and Tamasheq, became official languages.[2] The lingua franca in Mali is mainly Bambara, which about 80 percent of the population can communicate in.[4] Over 40 other African languages are spoken by the various ethnic groups of Mali.[4]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

The country is bordered to the north by Algeria, to the east by Niger, to the northwest by Mauritania, to the south by Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast, and to the west by Guinea and Senegal. <<A_RELEVANT>>The population of Mali is about 23.29 million,[14][15] 47.19% of which are estimated to be under the age of 15 in 2024.[16] Its capital and largest city is Bamako.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The country has 13 official languages, of which Bambara is the most commonly spoken.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In June 2023, Mali removed French as an official language with the approval of a new constitution by 97% of voters in a referendum conducted by the junta.[102]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Religion, the patriarchal norms, and gender-based violence are major negative factors shaping the life of women in Mali.[198] Patriarchal norms cause major gender inequalities and lead to male domination within the household.[198] Girls learn household activities like chores, cooking, childcare, etc. at a young age and are expected to take the main responsibility of household chores throughout their life.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>This hampers women's ability to enter the formal workforce and leads to a lack of education of girls.[198] Gender-based violence in Mali happens both on a national and a family level.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>At the national level, in 2012 the conflict in the Northern part of the country increased cases of kidnappings and rapes.[197] The conflict also reduced women's access to resources, economy, and opportunities.[197] At the household level, Malian women face gender-based violence through domestic violence, forced marriages, and marital rape.[196] The Demographic Health Survey for Mali in 2013 stated that 76% of women and 54% of men believed physical harm towards women was acceptable if the women burnt food, argued back, went out without notifying her husband, or refused sexual relations with her husband.[197] In 2024, Mali officials approved a bill criminalising intimate relations between same-sex couples.[199]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Mali's population encompasses a number of sub-Saharan ethnic groups.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The Bambara are by far the largest single ethnic group, making up a third of the population.[6] The largest ethnic groups are Bambara (33.3%), Fulani (Peuhl) (13.3%), Sarakole/Soninke/Marka (9.8%), Senufo/Manianka (9.6%), Malinke (8.8%), Dogon (8.7%), Sonrai (5.9%), Bobo (2.1%), Tuareg/Bella (1.7%), other Malian (6%), from members of Economic Community of West Africa (0.4%), other (0.3%) (2018 est.).[6] In Mali and in Niger, the Moors are also known as Azawagh Arabs, named after the Azawagh region of the Sahara.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>They speak mainly Hassaniya Arabic, one of the regional varieties of Arabic.[171]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Mali is also a member of the Organization for the Harmonization of Business Law in Africa (OHADA).[155] The gross domestic product (GDP) has risen since.<</QA_RELEVANT>> In 2002, the GDP amounted to US$3.4 billion,[156] and increased to US$5.8 billion in 2005,[153] which amounts to an approximately 17.6% annual growth rate.

<<QA_RELEVANT>>After adjusting the entrance requirements and access to education, girls still have lower enrollment rates and less access to formal education.[198] Drop-out rates for girls are 15% higher than that of boys because they have a higher responsibility at home and most parents refuse to allow all their children to go to school, so boys tend to become educated.[198] Similarly, technical and vocational education has a lower numbers of girls participating and are inadequately distributed in the country because the training centers are focused in the urban cities.[198] Finally, higher education for girls consist of short programs because early marriages prevent most girls from pursuing a longer term education program like those in science.[198] Although women do not have the same access of education, in recent decades women have been entering and representing in decision-making positions in the Public Administration sector.[198] Out of 147 members of Parliament, 15 were women in 2010.[198] Recent decades show that women are slowly joining important decision-making positions which is changing the attitude and status of women in Mali, which has led to the promotion of women's rights in the political sphere.[198]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The dynasty regrouped and defeated the Portuguese in 1613 and Siam in 1614.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>It restored a smaller, more manageable kingdom, encompassing Lower Myanmar, Upper Myanmar, Shan states, Lan Na and upper Tenasserim.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The restored Toungoo kings created a legal and political framework whose basic features continued well into the 19th century.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The crown completely replaced the hereditary chieftainships with appointed governorships in the entire Irrawaddy valley and greatly reduced the hereditary rights of Shan chiefs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its trade and secular administrative reforms built a prosperous economy for more than 80 years.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>From the 1720s onward, the kingdom was beset with repeated Meithei raids into Upper Myanmar and a nagging rebellion in Lan Na.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>In 1740, the Mon of Lower Myanmar founded the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Hanthawaddy forces sacked Ava in 1752, ending the 266-year-old Toungoo Dynasty.

In the north, the Hengduan Mountains form the border with China. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Hkakabo Razi, located in Kachin State, at an elevation of 5,881 metres (19,295 ft), is the highest point in Myanmar.[153] Many mountain ranges, such as the Rakhine Yoma, the Bago Yoma, the Shan Hills and the Tenasserim Hills exist within Myanmar, all of which run north-to-south from the Himalayas.[154] The mountain chains divide Myanmar's three river systems, which are the Irrawaddy, Salween (Thanlwin), and the Sittaung rivers.[155] The Irrawaddy River, Myanmar's longest river at nearly 2,170 kilometres (1,348 mi), flows into the Gulf of Martaban.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Fertile plains exist in the valleys between the mountain chains.[154] The majority of Myanmar's population lives in the Irrawaddy valley, which is situated between the Rakhine Yoma and the Shan Plateau.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Myanmar is divided into seven states (ပြည်နယ်) and seven regions (တိုင်းဒေသကြီး), formerly called divisions.[157] Regions are predominantly Bamar (that is, mainly inhabited by Myanmar's dominant ethnic group).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>States, in essence, are regions that are home to particular ethnic minorities.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The administrative divisions are further subdivided into districts, which are further subdivided into townships, wards, and villages.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Since 30 April 2022, districts inside regions and states have been expanded to total count of 121.[158]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Myanmar continues to perform badly in the global Environmental Performance Index (EPI) with an overall ranking of 153 out of 180 countries in 2016, among the worst in the South Asian region.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The environmental areas where Myanmar performs worst (i.e. highest ranking) are air quality (174), health impacts of environmental issues (143) and biodiversity and habitat (142).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Myanmar performs best (i.e. lowest ranking) in environmental impacts of fisheries (21) but with declining fish stocks.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Despite several issues, Myanmar also ranks 64 and scores very good (i.e. a high percentage of 93.73%) in environmental effects of the agricultural industry because of an excellent management of the nitrogen cycle.[164][165] Myanmar is one of the most highly vulnerable countries to climate change; this poses a number of social, political, economic and foreign policy challenges to the country.[166]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Ethnic identity in modern-day Myanmar has been significantly shaped by British colonial rule, Christian missionaries, and decolonisation in the post-independence era.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>To this day, the Burmese language does not have precise terminology that distinguishes the European concepts of race and ethnicity; the term lu-myo (လူမျိုး, lit. 'type of person') can reference race, ethnicity, and religion.[284] For instance, many Bamar self-identify as members of the 'Buddhist lu-myo' or the 'Myanmar lu-myo,' which has posed a significant challenge for census-takers.[285]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>British colonial rule introduced Western elements of culture to Myanmar.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Myanmar's education system is modelled after that of the United Kingdom.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Colonial architectural influences are most evident in major cities such as Yangon.[340] Many ethnic minorities, particularly the Karen in the southeast and the Kachin and Chin, who populate the far western state of Chin and the north and northeast, practice Christianity.[341] According to The World Factbook, the Burman population is 68% while other ethnic minorities groups constitute 32%.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In contrast, the exiled leaders and organizations claim the 40% of the population is composed of ethnic minorities.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Haiti
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>The two official languages of Haiti are French and Haitian Creole.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>French is the principal written and administratively authorized language (as well as the main language of the press) and is spoken by 42% of Haitians.[405][406] It is spoken by all educated Haitians, is the medium of instruction in most schools, and is used in the business sector.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is also used in ceremonial events such as weddings, graduations and church Masses.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Haiti is one of two independent nations in the Americas (along with Canada) to designate French as an official language; the other French-speaking areas are all overseas départements, or collectivités, of France, such as French Guiana.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Haitian Creole is spoken by nearly all of the Haitian population.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>French, the base language for Haitian Creole, is popular among the Haitian elite and upper classes.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>French is also popular in the business sector, and to a far lesser degree, English due to American influence.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Spanish is spoken by some Haitians who live along the Haitian-Dominican border.[407] English and Spanish may also be spoken by Haitian deportees from the United States and various Latin American countries.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Overall, about 90–95% of Haitians only speak Haitian Creole and French fluently, with over half only knowing Creole.[408]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The Armed Forces of Haiti (FAd'H) and the Haitian National Police (PNH) together officially make up the Public Force of Haiti,[297] whose personnel take an oath to the constitution and the flag of the country.[298] The Armed Forces consist of the land, sea, and air forces, along with technical support.[299] They are led by an active-duty general officer who is appointed as the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Haiti.[300] The Ministry of Defense is the main oversight body of the armed forces[301] while the police are part of the Ministry of Justice and Public Security.[302] The constitutional duties of the FA'dH include defending the country's borders, responding to natural disasters, and providing assistance to the police.[303] The 1987 constitution provides the basis for conscription,[304] though it has never been used.[305] The Armed Forces were disbanded in 1995 and security became solely the responsibility of the civilian National Police[306][307]  until 2017.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As of 2023 the Armed Forces had a strength of 2,000 service members, who were trained in nearby countries.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The military has had a small role during the gang war, which includes protecting government officials.[308]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The National Police was established in 1995 to replace the military's former role in law enforcement, initially recruited from among former military personnel and Haitian migrants to the United States.[309] In 1999 it had 6,000 members;[309]  in 2010, it numbered 7,000;[310] and in 2016 it had 9,000.[280] It is led by a director-general appointed by the president.[311] The PNH consists of the Administrative Police for day-to-day police work, the Judicial Police for investigations, and some specialized units that include presidential security, riot control, a SWAT team, and the Haitian Coast Guard.[312] Under-equipped and understaffed, it has been unable maintain security in the entire Haitian territory, despite some improvements to its capability by 2012.[313] Since the start of the gang war in 2020 the PNH has seen increasingly high levels of desertion and casualties.[279][308]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Haiti is a founding member of the United Nations, Organization of American States,[33] Association of Caribbean States,[34] and the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In addition to CARICOM, it is a member of the International Monetary Fund,[35] World Trade Organization,[36] and Community of Latin American and Caribbean States.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Haiti is a member of a wide range of international and regional organizations, such as the United Nations, CARICOM, Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, International Monetary Fund, Organisation of American States, Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, OPANAL and the World Trade Organization.[237]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The tourism market in Haiti is undeveloped, and the government is heavily promoting this sector.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Haiti has many of the features that attract tourists to other Caribbean destinations, such as white sand beaches, mountainous scenery and a year-round warm climate.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>However, the country's poor image overseas, at times exaggerated, has hampered the development of this sector.[51] In 2014, the country received 1,250,000 tourists (mostly from cruise ships), and the industry generated US$200 million in 2014.[citation needed]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

question: This nation includes a province named Limpopo, shares a border with Botswana, and its most populous urban area is Johannesburg. Using 2022 data, what is its health‑spending efficiency measured as life expectancy at birth (years) divided by health expenditure per capita (in constant 2011 US$) per $1,000?

entity_document.title: South Africa
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa (RSA), is the southernmost country in Africa.[d] Its nine provinces are bounded to the south by 2,798 kilometres (1,739 miles) of coastline that stretches along the South Atlantic and Indian Ocean;[16][17][18] to the north by the neighbouring countries of Namibia, Botswana, and Zimbabwe; to the east and northeast by Mozambique and Eswatini; and it encloses Lesotho.[19] Covering an area of 1,221,037 square kilometres (471,445 square miles), the country has a population of over 63 million people, making it the sixth-most populated country in Africa.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Pretoria is the administrative capital, while Cape Town, as the seat of Parliament, is the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein is regarded as the judicial capital.[20] The largest and most populous city is Johannesburg, followed by Cape Town and Durban.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>South Africa is a parliamentary republic, but unlike most such republics, the president is both head of state and head of government and depends for their tenure on the confidence of Parliament.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The executive, legislature, and judiciary are all subject to the supremacy of the Constitution of South Africa, and the superior courts have the power to strike down executive actions and acts of Parliament if they are unconstitutional.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The National Assembly, the lower house of Parliament, consists of 400 members and is elected every five years by a system of party-list proportional representation.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The National Council of Provinces, the upper house, consists of ninety members, with each of the nine provincial legislatures electing ten members.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>South Africa has a generally temperate climate because it is surrounded by the Atlantic and Indian Oceans on three sides, because it is located in the climatically milder Southern Hemisphere, and because its average elevation rises steadily toward the north (toward the equator) and further inland.<</QA_RELEVANT>> This varied topography and oceanic influence result in a great variety of climatic zones. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The climatic zones range from the extreme desert of the southern Namib in the farthest northwest to the lush subtropical climate in the east along the border with Mozambique and the Indian Ocean.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Winters in South Africa occur between June and August.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The extreme southwest has a climate similar to that of the Mediterranean with wet winters and hot, dry summers, hosting the famous fynbos biome of shrubland and thicket.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>This area produces much of the wine in South Africa and is known for its wind, which blows intermittently almost all year.<</QA_RELEVANT>> The severity of this wind made passing around the Cape of Good Hope particularly treacherous for sailors, causing many shipwrecks. Further east on the south coast, rainfall is distributed more evenly throughout the year, producing a green landscape. The annual rainfall increases south of the Lowveld, especially near the coast, which is subtropical. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Free State is particularly flat because it lies centrally on the high plateau.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>North of the Vaal River, the Highveld becomes better watered and does not experience subtropical extremes of heat.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Johannesburg, in the centre of the Highveld, is at 1,740 m (5,709 ft) above sea level and receives an annual rainfall of 760 mm (29.9 in).<</Q_RELEVANT>> Winters in this region are cold, although snow is rare.[131]

<<QA_RELEVANT>>South Africa has no legally defined capital city.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The fourth chapter of the constitution states "The seat of Parliament is Cape Town, but an Act of Parliament enacted in accordance with section 76(1) and (5) may determine that the seat of Parliament is elsewhere."[156] The country's three branches of government are split over different cities.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Cape Town, as the seat of Parliament, is the legislative capital; Pretoria, as the seat of the president and cabinet, is the administrative capital; and Bloemfontein is the seat of the Supreme Court of Appeal, and is regarded as the judicial capital;[20] although the highest court, the Constitutional Court of South Africa has been based in Johannesburg since 1994.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Most foreign embassies are located in Pretoria.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Other languages are spoken, or were widely used previously, including Fanagalo, Khoe, Lobedu, Nama, Northern Ndebele, and Phuthi.[341] Many of the unofficial languages of the San and Khoekhoe peoples contain regional dialects stretching northwards into Namibia and Botswana, and elsewhere.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>These people, who are a physically distinct population from the Bantu people who make up most of the Black Africans in South Africa, have their own cultural identity based on their hunter-gatherer societies.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>They have been marginalised, and the remainder of their languages are in danger of becoming extinct.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The South African media sector is large, and South Africa is one of Africa's major media centres.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>While the many broadcasters and publications reflect the diversity of the population as a whole, the most commonly used language is English.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, all ten other official languages are represented to some extent.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Germany
entity_document.text:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The president, who has been Frank-Walter Steinmeier since 2017, is the head of state and invested primarily with representative responsibilities and powers.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He is elected by the Bundesversammlung (federal convention), an institution consisting of the members of the Bundestag and an equal number of state delegates.[115] The second-highest official in the German order of precedence is the Bundestagspräsident (president of the Bundestag), who is elected by the Bundestag and responsible for overseeing the daily sessions of the body.[134] The third-highest official and the head of government is the chancellor, who is appointed by the Bundespräsident after being elected by the party or coalition with the most seats in the Bundestag.[115] The chancellor, who has been Friedrich Merz since 2025, is the head of government and exercises executive power through his Cabinet.[115]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Germany is a federal, parliamentary, representative democratic republic.[115] Federal legislative power is vested in the parliament consisting of the Bundestag (Federal Diet) and Bundesrat (Federal Council), which together form the legislative body.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Bundestag is elected through direct elections using the mixed-member proportional representation system.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The members of the Bundesrat represent and are appointed by the governments of the sixteen federated states.[115]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Germany,[d] officially the Federal Republic of Germany,[e] is a country in Western and Central Europe.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It lies between the Baltic Sea and the North Sea to the north with the Alps to the south.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its sixteen constituent states have a total population of over 82 million, making it the most populous member state of the European Union.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Germany borders Denmark to the north; Poland and the Czech Republic to the east; Austria and Switzerland to the south; and France, Luxembourg, Belgium, and the Netherlands to the west.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The nation's capital and most populous city is Berlin and its main financial centre is Frankfurt; the largest urban area is the Ruhr.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Unification of Germany into the modern nation-state, led by Prussia, established the German Empire in 1871.<</QA_RELEVANT>> After World War I and a revolution, the Empire was replaced by the Weimar Republic. The Nazi rise to power in 1933 led to the establishment of a totalitarian dictatorship, World War II, and the Holocaust. <<QA_RELEVANT>>In 1949, after the war and Allied occupation, Germany was organised into two separate polities with limited sovereignty: the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG), or West Germany, and the German Democratic Republic (GDR), or East Germany.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The FRG was a founding member of the European Economic Community, while the GDR was a communist Eastern Bloc state and a founding member of the Warsaw Pact.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>After the fall of the communist led-government in East Germany, German reunification saw the former East German states join the FRG on 3 October 1990.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Germany has a network of 227 diplomatic missions abroad[154] and maintains relations with more than 190 countries.[155] Germany is a member of the Council of Europe, NATO, the OECD, the G7, the G20, the World Bank and the IMF.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It has played an influential role in the European Union since its inception[156] and has maintained a strong alliance with France[157] and all neighbouring countries since 1990.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Germany promotes the creation of a more unified European political, economic and security apparatus.[158] Because of its economic power and political influence, Germany is widely considered to be a great power.[159][160]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The worldwide Great Depression hit Germany in 1929, and by 1932 the unemployment rate had risen to 24%.[69] The Nazi Party led by Adolf Hitler became the largest party in the Reichstag after the election of July 1932, and President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933.[70] After the Reichstag fire, a decree abrogated basic civil rights, and the first Nazi concentration camp opened.[71][72] On 23 March 1933, the Enabling Act gave Hitler unrestricted legislative power, overriding the constitution,[73] and marked the beginning of Nazi Germany.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>His government established a centralised totalitarian state, withdrew from the League of Nations, and dramatically increased the country's rearmament.[74] A government-sponsored programme for economic renewal focused on public works, the most famous of which was the Autobahn.[75]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: Consider a nation in East Africa that is a member of the African Union, contains the Dar es Salaam Region, and where Swahili is an official language. Using 2022 data, compute its economic‑complexity proxy defined as trade openness (the sum of exports and imports as a share of GDP) multiplied by log₁₀(GDP per capita) plus the share of foreign direct investment inflows in GDP. Report the resulting score rounded to two decimal places.

entity_document.title: Tanzania
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>Tanganyika joined the British Commonwealth and Tanzania remains a member of the Commonwealth as a unified republic.[17] Today, the country is a presidential constitutional republic with the federal capital located in Government City (Dodoma);[18] the former capital, Dar es Salaam, retains most government offices and is the country's largest city, principal port, and leading commercial centre.[16][19][20] For decades, Tanzania has been ruled by the Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) as a de facto one-party state.[21][22]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Tanzania is mountainous and densely forested in the north-east, where Mount Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa and the highest single free-standing mountain above sea level in the world, is located.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Three of the African Great Lakes are partly within Tanzania.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>To the north and west lie Lake Victoria, Africa's largest lake, and Lake Tanganyika, the continent's deepest lake, known for its unique species of fish.<</Q_RELEVANT>> To the south lies Lake Malawi. The eastern shore is hot and humid, with the Zanzibar Archipelago just offshore. The Menai Bay Conservation Area is Zanzibar's largest marine protected area. <<QA_RELEVANT>>The Kalambo Falls, located on the Kalambo River at the Zambian border, is the second-highest uninterrupted waterfall in Africa.[27] Tanzania is one of the most visited tourist destinations for safaris.[28] The country is an official member of the United Nations, Group of 77, African Union, East African Community, and the Non-Aligned Movement.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Tanzania's population comprises about 120 ethnic,[23] linguistic, and religious groups.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Christianity is the largest religion in Tanzania, with substantial Muslim and Animist minorities.[24] Over 100 languages are spoken in Tanzania, making it the most linguistically diverse country in East Africa.[25] The country does not have a de jure official language,[2] although the national language is Swahili.[4] English is used in foreign trade, in diplomacy, in higher courts, and as a medium of instruction in secondary and higher education.[25][26] Arabic is widely spoken in Zanzibar, reflecting its history as a trading center dominated by Arabs.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The East African Community consisting of Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is headquartered in Arusha.[141][142] Tanzania, along with Kenya and Uganda, is a founding member of the EAC in 2000.[143] Following the German defeat in World War I Tanzania joined the London-based East African Currency Board (EACB) that was a customs union and provider of currency for Tanzania, Uganda, and Kenya from 1919 to 1948, the East Africa High Commission (EAHC) from 1948 to 1961, and East African Common Services Organization (EACSO) from 1961 to 1966.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1966 all three countries formed the first East African Community, which lasted until 1976, then the East African Co-operation from 1993 to 2000, before becoming reestablished as the East African Community in 2000.[143][144]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The EAC has had a customs union since 2005, with a free trade zone between member states and unified tariffs and trade agreements with non-member states and multinational organizations.[141] The customs union also established a unified organization and sets of rules, such as rules of origin, for all trade within, into, and passing through member states.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2010 a common market was established within the EAC for the free movement of labor, goods, people, capital, and services, as well as established rights of establishment.[141] The East African Monetary Union (EAMU) proposed to be established in 2024 that will create a single common currency by the East African Central Bank.[145] From the original reestablishment of the EAC, as laid out in Article 5(2) of the Treaty for the Establishment of the East African Community, the final goal for the EAC is always the political federation of all member states.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2017 all member states adopted the confederation of EAC as a transitional precursor to the final federation.[141][144]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Growth in Egyptian and Persian shipping from the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf revitalised Indian Ocean trade, particularly after the Fatimid Caliphate relocated to Fustat (Cairo).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Swahili agriculturalists built increasingly dense settlements to tap into trade, these forming the earliest Swahili city-states.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The Venda-Shona Kingdoms of Mapungubwe and Zimbabwe in South Africa and Zimbabwe, respectively, became a major producer of gold around this same period. <<QA_RELEVANT>>Economic, social, and religious power was increasingly vested in Kilwa, Tanzania's major medieval city-state.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Kilwa controlled a number of smaller ports stretching down to modern-day Mozambique.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Sofala became the major gold emporium and Kilwa grew rich off the trade, lying at the southern end of the Indian Ocean Monsoons. Kilwa's major rivals lay to the north, in modern-day Kenya, namely Mombasa and Malindi. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Kilwa remained the major power in East Africa until the arrival of the Portuguese at the end of the 15th century.[39]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Pakistan,[f] officially the Islamic Republic of Pakistan,[g] is a country in South Asia.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is the fifth-most populous country, with a population of over 241.5 million,[d] having the second-largest Muslim population as of 2023.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Islamabad is the nation's capital, while Karachi is its largest city and financial centre.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Pakistan is the 33rd-largest country by area.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Bounded by the Arabian Sea on the south, the Gulf of Oman on the southwest, and the Sir Creek on the southeast, it shares land borders with India to the east; Afghanistan to the west; Iran to the southwest; and China to the northeast.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It shares a maritime border with Oman in the Gulf of Oman, and is separated from Tajikistan in the northwest by Afghanistan's narrow Wakhan Corridor.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Pakistan is a diverse society with estimates suggesting it has between 75 and 85 languages.[513][514] Urdu and English serve as the official languages, with Urdu being the country's lingua franca and a unifying force among over 75% of Pakistanis.[515][516] According to the 2023 national census, the largest ethnolinguistic groups include the Punjabis (36.98%), Pashtuns (18.15%), Sindhis (14.31%), Saraikis (12%), Urdu speaking people (9.25%), Balochs (3.38%), Hindkowans/Hazarewals (2.32%), and Brahuis (1.16%).[517][518] The remaining population consists of various ethnic minorities such as Kashmiris, Paharis, Chitralis, various peoples of Gilgit-Baltistan, Kohistanis, Torwalis, Meos, Hazaras, Kalash and Siddis.[519][520] The Pakistani diaspora, numbering over seven million, is the sixth largest in the world.[521]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Pakistan's diverse geography and climate host a wide array of wildlife.[165] Covering 881,913 km2 (340,509 sq mi),[166] Pakistan ranks as the 33rd-largest nation by total area,[167] but this varies based on Kashmir's disputed status.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Pakistan boasts a 1,046 km (650 mi) coastline along the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman,[168][169] and shares land borders totaling 6,774 km (4,209 mi), including 2,430 km (1,510 mi) with Afghanistan, 523 km (325 mi) with China, 2,912 km (1,809 mi) with India, and 909 km (565 mi) with Iran.[170] It has a maritime border with Oman[171] and is separated from Tajikistan via the narrow strip of the Wakhan Corridor.[172] Situated at the crossroads of South Asia, the Middle East, and Central Asia,[173] Pakistan's location is geopolitically significant.[174] Geologically, Pakistan lies at the interaction of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates within the Indus–Tsangpo Suture Zone, a region of high seismic activity.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The collision between these two plates occurs in northwest Pakistan, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Sindh and Punjab are located on the north-western corner of the Indian Plate, while Balochistan and much of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa lie along its north-western margin.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Northern areas of Pakistan, including Azad Kashmir, lie along the northern edge of the Indian Plate and are prone to powerful earthquakes.[175]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Pakistan, a federal parliamentary republic, consists of four provinces: Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, and Balochistan, along with three territories: Islamabad Capital Territory, Gilgit-Baltistan, and Azad Kashmir.[277] The Government of Pakistan governs the western parts of the Kashmir Region, organized into separate political entities, Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan.[278] In 2009, the constitutional assignment (the Gilgit–Baltistan Empowerment and Self-Governance Order) granted Gilgit-Baltistan semi-provincial status, providing it with self-government.[279]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Spurred by the Pakistan Movement, which sought a homeland for the Muslims of British India, and election victories in 1946 by the All-India Muslim League, Pakistan gained independence in 1947 after the partition of British India, which awarded separate statehood to its Muslim-majority regions and was accompanied by an unparalleled mass migration and loss of life.[12][13] Initially a dominion of the British Commonwealth, Pakistan adopted a republican constitution in 1956 and became an Islamic republic with two geographically separate provinces, East Pakistan and West Pakistan.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>East Pakistan seceded as the new country of Bangladesh in 1971 after a nine-month-long civil war.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>In the following four decades, Pakistan has been ruled by governments that alternated between civilian and military, democratic and authoritarian, relatively secular and Islamist.[14]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, commonly known as the United Kingdom (UK) or Britain,[m] is a country in northwestern Europe, off the coast of the continental mainland.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It comprises England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland,[n] with a population of over 69 million in 2024.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The UK includes the island of Great Britain, the north-eastern part of the island of Ireland, and most of the smaller islands within the British Isles, covering 94,354 square miles (244,376 km2).[f] It shares a land border with the Republic of Ireland and is surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean, the North Sea, the English Channel, the Celtic Sea and the Irish Sea, while maintaining sovereignty over the Crown Dependencies and the British Overseas Territories.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The capital and largest city of England and the UK is London; Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast are the national capitals of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The United Kingdom is said to have a "Special Relationship" with the United States and a close partnership with France – the "Entente cordiale" – and shares nuclear weapons technology with both countries;[233][234] the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance is considered to be the oldest binding military alliance in the world.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The UK is also closely linked with the Republic of Ireland; the two countries share a Common Travel Area and co-operate through the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference and the British-Irish Council.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Britain's global presence and influence is further amplified through its trading relations, foreign investments, official development assistance and military engagements.[235]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2001, over 92,000 people in Scotland, just under 2 per cent of the population, had some Gaelic language ability, including 72 per cent of those living in the Outer Hebrides.[375] The number of children being taught either Welsh or Scottish Gaelic is increasing.[376] Scots, a language descended from early northern Middle English, has limited recognition alongside its regional variant, Ulster Scots in Northern Ireland, without specific commitments to protection and promotion.[2][377] As of April 2020 there are around 151,000 users of British Sign Language (BSL), a sign language used by deaf people, in the UK.[378]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The modern system of universal publicly funded healthcare in the United Kingdom has its origins in the creation of the National Health Service (NHS) in 1949 is the primary healthcare provider in the United Kingdom.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The widespread popularity of the NHS has led to it being described as a "national religion".[417][418] Healthcare in the United Kingdom is a devolved matter and each country has its own system of universal publicly funded healthcare (NHS England, NHS Scotland, Health and Social Care (Northern Ireland) and NHS Wales), although private healthcare is also available.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Public healthcare is provided to all UK permanent residents and is mostly free at the point of need, being paid for from general taxation.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The World Health Organization, in 2000, ranked the provision of healthcare in the United Kingdom as fifteenth-best in Europe and eighteenth in the world.[419]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>A poll in 2003 found that football is the most popular sport in the UK.[524] England is recognised by FIFA as the birthplace of club football, and the Football Association is the oldest of its kind, with the rules of football first drafted in 1863 by Ebenezer Cobb Morley.[525] Each of the Home Nations (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland) has its own football association, national team and league system, and each is individually a governing member of the International Football Association Board alongside FIFA.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The English top division, the Premier League, is the most watched football league in the world.[526] The first international football match was contested by England and Scotland on 30 November 1872.[527] England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland usually compete as separate countries in international competitions.[528]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The main political parties of the 19th century were the Catholic Party and the Liberal Party, with the Belgian Labour Party emerging towards the end of the 19th century. <<Q_RELEVANT>>French was originally the official language used by the nobility and the bourgeoisie, especially after the rejection of the Dutch monarchy.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>French progressively lost its dominance as Dutch began to recover its status.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This recognition became official in 1898, and in 1967, the parliament accepted a Dutch version of the Constitution.[47]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Following the campaigns of 1794 in the French Revolutionary Wars, the Low Countries – including territories that were never nominally under Habsburg rule, such as the Prince-Bishopric of Liège – were annexed by the French First Republic, ending Austrian rule in the region.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After the dissolution of the First French Empire and the abdication of Napoleon following his defeat on the battlefield of Waterloo, the Congress of Vienna in 1814–15 created the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This buffer state, located between the major European powers, united the former territories of the Dutch Republic, the Austrian Netherlands and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, under King William I of Orange.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Belgium is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy with a complex federal system structured on regional and linguistic grounds.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The country is divided into three highly autonomous regions:[15] the Flemish Region (Flanders) in the north, the Walloon Region (Wallonia) in the south, and the Brussels-Capital Region in the middle.[16] Belgium is also home to two main linguistic communities: the Dutch-speaking Flemish Community, which constitutes about 60 percent of the population, and the French-speaking French Community,[e] which constitutes about 40 percent of the population; a small German-speaking Community, comprising around one percent of the population, exists in the East Cantons.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Belgium's linguistic diversity and related political conflicts are reflected in its complex system of governance, made up of six different governments.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Belgium is a developed country with an advanced high-income economy.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is one of the six founding members of the European Union, with its capital of Brussels serving as the de facto capital of the EU, hosting the official seats of the European Commission, the Council of the European Union, the European Council, and one of two seats of the European Parliament (the other being Strasbourg).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Brussels also hosts the headquarters of many major international organizations, such as NATO.[f]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The King (currently Philippe) is the head of state, though with limited prerogatives.<</Q_RELEVANT>> He appoints ministers, including a Prime Minister, that have the confidence of the Chamber of Representatives to form the federal government. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Council of Ministers is composed of no more than fifteen members.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>With the possible exception of the Prime Minister, the Council of Ministers is composed of an equal number of Dutch-speaking members and French-speaking members.[76]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, French and German.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>A number of non-official minority languages are spoken as well.[183] As no census exists, there are no official statistical data regarding the distribution or usage of Belgium's three official languages or their dialects.[184] However, various criteria, including the language(s) of parents, of education, or the second-language status of foreign born, may provide suggested figures.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>An estimated 60% of the Belgian population are native speakers of Dutch (often referred to as Flemish), and 40% of the population speaks French natively.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>French-speaking Belgians are often referred to as Walloons, although the French speakers in Brussels are not Walloons.[p]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>A major non-official holiday is Saint Nicholas Day (Dutch: Sinterklaas, French: la Saint-Nicolas), a festivity for children, and in Liège, for students.[230] It takes place each year on 6 December and is a sort of early Christmas.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>On the evening of 5 December, before going to bed, children put their shoes by the hearth with water or wine and a carrot for Saint Nicholas' horse or donkey.<</Q_RELEVANT>> According to tradition, Saint Nicholas comes at night and travels down the chimney. <<Q_RELEVANT>>He then takes the food and water or wine, leaves presents, goes back up, feeds his horse or donkey, and continues on his course.<</Q_RELEVANT>> He also knows whether children have been good or bad. <<QA_RELEVANT>>This holiday is especially loved by children in Belgium and the Netherlands.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Dutch immigrants imported the tradition into the United States, where Saint Nicholas is now known as Santa Claus.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The country adopted the euro in 2001 and successfully hosted the 2004 Summer Olympic Games in Athens.[141] In 2010, Greece suffered from the Great Recession and related Euro area crisis.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Due to the adoption of the euro, Greece could no longer devalue its currency to regain competitiveness.[142] In the 2012 elections, there was major political change, with new parties emerging from the collapse of the two main parties, PASOK and New Democracy.[143] In 2015, Alexis Tsipras was elected as prime minister, the first outside the two main parties.[144] The Greek government-debt crisis, and subsequent austerity policies, resulted in social strife.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The crisis ended around 2018, with the end of the bailout mechanisms and return of growth.[145] Simultaneously, Tsipras, and the leader of North Macedonia, Zoran Zaev, signed the Prespa Agreement, solving the naming dispute that had strained the relations and eased the latter's way to become a member of the EU and NATO.[146]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Almost two-thirds of the Greek people live in urban areas.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Greece's largest and most influential metropolitan centres are Athens (population 3,744,059 according to 2021 census) and Thessaloniki (population 1,092,919 in 2021) that latter commonly referred to as the symprotévousa (συμπρωτεύουσα, lit. 'co-capital').[305] Other prominent cities with populations above 100,000 inhabitants include Patras, Heraklion, Larissa, Volos, Rhodes, Ioannina, Agrinio, Chania, and Chalcis.[306]<</QA_RELEVANT>>
